lessons.title: Hat jemand ein Zelt?: planning a festival with jemand, niemand, alle
lessons.goal: Plan a festival visit together and talk about people without names: someone, no one, everyone, many, some.

grammar.topic: jemand, niemand, alle, viele, einige, man
grammar.point: People without a name: jemand (someone), niemand (no one) and man (people in general) take a SINGULAR verb, like er: Niemand hat Zeit. alle, viele, einige take a PLURAL verb: Alle kommen mit. niemand already means no: never add nicht.
grammar.oneLine: Hat jemand ein Zelt? – Nein, niemand.

mistake.why: niemand and jemand take the singular verb, like er, sie, es.

terms.meaning: a word for a person or thing without a name: jemand, niemand, etwas, nichts
someone / no one: singular verb (Jemand hat …)
everyone / many / some: plural verb (Alle kommen.)

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Mira hat Zeit' to 'Hat jemand Zeit?'
cards.body: This last A2 chapter is called Gute Unterhaltung! (Enjoy the show!). It is about music, festivals and pictures. First the WG plans a weekend at the Sommerfestival near Kiel. Leon asks the big questions: Who comes? Who has a tent? When you do not know the name of the person, you need new little words: jemand, niemand, alle.
steps: You already know: Mira hat Zeit. Alle Leute sind da. Man braucht Tickets.
New today: Hat jemand ein Zelt? Niemand hat Zeit. Alle kommen mit. jemand and niemand take a singular verb, alle, viele and einige a plural verb.
By the end you can: plan a festival weekend, ask who has something, and talk about people without names.

examples.de: Mira hat Zeit.
examples.en: Mira has time.
examples.why: You know this: a name and a normal verb.

examples.de: Hat jemand Zeit?
examples.en: Does anyone have time?
examples.why: New today: jemand = someone, a person without a name.

cards.more: Think of a dark room before a concert. You hear a voice, but you cannot see who it is. In German you say: Jemand ist da (someone is there). If the room is empty: Niemand ist da (no one is there). If the whole WG is in the room: Alle sind da. Today you learn these words for people without a face, and which verb form goes with each one.

cards.title: The festival plan
cards.body: Every plan answers four questions: Wann? Wo? Was kostet es? Wer kommt mit? The Sommerfestival is from Friday to Sunday. The ticket (die Eintrittskarte) costs 89 Euro. The WG sleeps in a tent on the campsite (der Campingplatz). The last question, Wer kommt mit?, needs today's new words.
cards.lead: Before the grammar, we make the plan. These are the facts and the new words of the weekend, so that every example later in the lesson makes sense.

examples.de: Das Sommerfestival ist von Freitag bis Sonntag.
examples.en: The summer festival is from Friday to Sunday.

examples.de: Die Eintrittskarte kostet 89 Euro.
examples.en: The ticket costs 89 euros.

examples.de: Wir schlafen im Zelt auf dem Campingplatz.
examples.en: We sleep in the tent on the campsite.

deeper.text: der Eintritt is the entry and the price for it; die Eintrittskarte is the ticket you hold in your hand. On posters you often read Eintritt frei! (free entry). Young people also say das Ticket, which you know. At big German festivals you often get a band for your wrist instead of a paper ticket, but people still ask: Hast du deine Eintrittskarte?

example.de: Der Eintritt für Kinder ist frei.
example.en: Entry for children is free.

cards.more: Imagine a sticky note on the fridge with four lines. Wann? Freitag bis Sonntag. Wo? Bei Kiel. Was kostet es? 89 Euro. Wer kommt mit? Only the last line is still empty. That is how every plan in German starts: three facts are easy, and the people question is open. In English you would ask Who is coming? In German: Wer kommt mit? The answer to this question is today's grammar.
steps: Wann? Von Freitag bis Sonntag.
Wo? Auf dem Campingplatz bei Kiel.
Was kostet es? Die Eintrittskarte kostet 89 Euro.
Wer kommt mit? (jemand, niemand, alle …)

cards.title: jemand and niemand
cards.body: jemand = someone or anyone. niemand = no one. You use them when you do not know or do not say the name. The verb is singular, the same form as for er, sie, es: Jemand hat … , Niemand kommt. In a question, jemand means anyone: Hat jemand eine Taschenlampe?
cards.lead: The plan is ready, but who has the things? Now we learn the two words for a person without a name: jemand for someone, niemand for no one.

examples.de: Hat jemand eine Taschenlampe?
examples.en: Does anyone have a torch?

examples.de: Niemand hat einen Schlafsack.
examples.en: No one has a sleeping bag.

examples.de: Kommt jemand mit? – Nein, niemand.
examples.en: Is anyone coming along? – No, no one.

deeper.text: When jemand or niemand is the object, careful German adds -en: Ich sehe niemanden. Kennst du hier jemanden? In everyday speech many people drop the ending, and both are understood. For now, just recognise the -en form when you read it. In this course you use jemand and niemand as the subject, where they never change.

example.de: Kennst du hier jemanden?
example.en: Do you know anyone here?

cards.more: jemand and niemand are like a person in a big winter coat with the hood up: you see someone, but not who. Because it is one person, the verb is the same as for er or sie: er hat, jemand hat, niemand hat. English works the same: someone has, no one has. So whenever you would say he or she in English, you can put jemand or niemand in the same place.

cards.title: niemand already says no
cards.body: niemand already contains the no. So you never add nicht or kein: Niemand ist zu Hause. A short answer works too: Wer hat Zeit? – Niemand. The opposite is jemand: Jemand ruft an. If you are alone somewhere, say: Hier ist niemand.
cards.lead: niemand is a no-word. Before we practise, we make sure you do not say no twice, because that is a mistake learners make very often.

examples.de: Niemand ist zu Hause.
examples.en: No one is at home.

examples.de: Hier ist niemand.
examples.en: No one is here.

examples.de: Jemand ruft an.
examples.en: Someone is calling.

deeper.text: Two small time words make jemand and niemand very natural: schon and noch. Ist schon jemand da? asks: Is anyone there yet? The answer Nein, noch niemand means: No, nobody yet, but people will come. You hear this all the time before a concert or a party. noch niemand is softer than niemand: it says the situation will change soon.

example.de: Ist schon jemand da? – Nein, noch niemand.
example.en: Is anyone there yet? – No, nobody yet.

cards.more: Think of a light switch with only one switch for no. niemand already turns the light off. If you add nicht, you press the switch again, and the light is on again. That is why Niemand kommt nicht. is wrong: say Niemand kommt. English has the same rule in good English: No one comes, not No one doesn't come. One no-word per sentence is enough.

cards.title: alle, viele, einige: plural verb
cards.body: For groups you need other words: alle (everyone), viele (many), einige (some, a few). They mean many people, so the verb is plural, like for wir and sie: Alle kommen mit. Viele fahren mit dem Zug. jemand, niemand and man take the singular verb.
cards.lead: jemand and niemand are one person. Now we look at the words for groups of people, and here the verb changes to the plural form.

examples.de: Alle kommen mit.
examples.en: Everyone is coming along.

examples.de: Viele fahren mit dem Zug.
examples.en: Many are going by train.

examples.de: Einige schlafen im Auto.
examples.en: Some are sleeping in the car.

deeper.text: Germans often put alle later in the sentence, after the verb: Wir kommen alle mit. Sie sind alle da. This sounds very natural and means the same as Alle kommen mit. With a pronoun like wir or sie, this is the usual place for alle. You also know alle as a word before a noun: alle Leute, alle Freunde. There the verb is plural too.

example.de: Wir kommen alle mit.
example.en: We are all coming along.

cards.more: Picture a full bus, a half-full bus, a bus with three people and an empty bus. Full bus: alle. Half full: viele. Three people: einige. Empty: niemand. The first three are groups, so you count them like sie (they): sie kommen, alle kommen, einige kommen. The empty bus is like one person who is not there: niemand kommt. In English it is the same: many are, some are, no one is.

cards.title: man: people in general
cards.body: You know man from A1: it means people in general, you, one. man is also singular: Man braucht Gummistiefel. man is a rule for everyone, jemand is one person you do not know. On a festival you hear music everywhere (überall): Auf dem Festival hört man überall Musik.
cards.lead: jemand is one unknown person. Now we repeat man, which you know, and see how it is different: man talks about everyone in general, like a rule.

examples.de: Man braucht Gummistiefel.
examples.en: You need rubber boots.

examples.de: Auf dem Festival hört man überall Musik.
examples.en: At the festival you hear music everywhere.

examples.de: Man darf kein Glas mitbringen.
examples.en: You are not allowed to bring glass.

deeper.text: In a long sentence you repeat man; you never switch to er: Man braucht ein Zelt, wenn man auf dem Campingplatz schläft. English can say you … you or one … one; German keeps man. man also exists only as the subject. Festival rules on posters often use man with dürfen: Man darf kein Glas mitbringen. That is the polite way to give a rule.

example.de: Man braucht ein Zelt, wenn man auf dem Campingplatz schläft.
example.en: You need a tent if you sleep on the campsite.

cards.more: Imagine a sign at the festival gate. It does not talk to Ben or to Mira, it talks to every visitor: Man darf kein Glas mitbringen. That is man: everyone, no name. Now imagine Ben in the tent hears a voice outside: Jemand ist draußen! That is one real person he cannot see. So: a rule for all people is man, one unknown person is jemand. Both take the er-form of the verb.

cards.title: In the WG kitchen: Wer kommt mit?
cards.body: Now the whole WG plans together. Leon asks, Mira answers for everyone, and Ben has the tent question. Read the six lines and look at the verbs: alle with plural, jemand and niemand with singular. Leon needs a big tent: ein großes Zelt, with the ending you know.
cards.lead: You have all the words now. In this mini dialogue the WG uses them together, the way you will use them when you plan with friends.

examples.de: Hat jemand ein Zelt?
examples.en: Does anyone have a tent?

examples.de: Nein, niemand. Aber Frau Weber hat ein Zelt.
examples.en: No, no one. But Frau Weber has a tent.

examples.de: Wir brauchen ein großes Zelt.
examples.en: We need a big tent.

deeper.text: The chapter title is a fixed phrase: Gute Unterhaltung! You say it to someone before a film, a concert or a show, like Enjoy the show! For friends, Viel Spaß! is more casual. Unterhaltung has a second meaning: a conversation. Wir hatten eine nette Unterhaltung means We had a nice chat. And Kommst du mit? is the classic way to invite someone to come along.

example.de: Gute Unterhaltung!
example.en: Enjoy the show!

cards.more: Read the dialogue like a little play in the kitchen. Leon is the planner with his list. Mira is happy and says Alle! for the whole group. Ben thinks about the night and asks about the tent. Anna knows that nobody in the WG has one, but she remembers Frau Weber. Then Leon has the plan: fragen wir sie. When you plan with friends, you need exactly these questions and answers.

rows: Nein, niemand. Aber Frau Weber hat ein Zelt.

lessons.title: Hast du etwas gegen Mücken?: asking for something with etwas, nichts, alles
lessons.goal: Ask for things you need and answer with something, nothing or everything, and ask politely.

grammar.point: Things without a name: etwas (something), nichts (nothing), alles (everything); they never change. alles takes a SINGULAR verb (Alles ist nass.), alle (people) a PLURAL verb (Alle sind nass.). viel / wenig + a noun without article: viel Wasser, wenig Geld.
grammar.oneLine: Hast du etwas gegen Mücken? – Tut mir leid, ich habe nichts dabei.

mistake.why: Things = alles + singular verb; people = alle + plural verb.

terms.meaning: something / nothing: for things, never changes
everything (singular verb) vs everyone (plural verb)
to have with you: Ich habe nichts dabei.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'jemand' (people) to 'etwas' (things)
cards.body: Friday evening on the campsite. The tent stands, the music starts, and Ben opens his rucksack: it is almost empty. Now he must ask the others for things all weekend. For people without a name you learnt jemand and niemand. For things without a name you need etwas (something), nichts (nothing) and alles (everything).
steps: You already know: Hat jemand eine Taschenlampe? Kannst du mir helfen? Könntest du …?
New today: Hast du etwas gegen Kopfschmerzen? Ich habe nichts dabei. Alles ist nass. alles takes a singular verb, alle a plural verb.
By the end you can: ask for things you need, answer with something, nothing or everything, and ask politely.

examples.de: Hat jemand eine Taschenlampe?
examples.en: Does anyone have a torch?
examples.why: You know this: jemand is a person.

examples.de: Hast du etwas gegen Kopfschmerzen?
examples.en: Do you have something for a headache?
examples.why: New today: etwas is a thing, not a person.

cards.more: Imagine two boxes. In the first box are people: jemand, niemand, alle. You filled it in the last lesson. The second box is for things, and today you fill it: etwas, nichts, alles. The two boxes look alike, like twins: jemand and etwas, niemand and nichts, alle and alles. If you know which box you need, a person or a thing, you know the word.

cards.title: People or things?
cards.body: Each people word has a partner for things. jemand (someone) → etwas (something). niemand (no one) → nichts (nothing). alle (everyone) → alles (everything). Ask yourself first: Is it a person or a thing? Then choose the word. Both can be in one sentence: Niemand hört etwas.
cards.lead: In lesson 1 you talked about people without names. Now we put a twin next to each people word: the word for a thing without a name.

examples.de: Jemand ist im Zelt.
examples.en: Someone is in the tent.

examples.de: Etwas ist im Zelt.
examples.en: Something is in the tent.

examples.de: Niemand hört etwas.
examples.en: No one hears anything.

deeper.text: In everyday speech Germans often shorten etwas to was: Hast du was gegen Mücken? Möchtest du was trinken? This was is not the question word, it simply means something. You will hear it all the time, and in a text message it looks very normal. In writing to Frau Weber or in an exam, use the full form etwas.

example.de: Möchtest du was trinken?
example.en: Would you like something to drink?

cards.more: Think of a torch in the dark tent. You hear a noise. Is it a person or a thing? If it is a person, you whisper: Jemand ist im Zelt! If it is a thing, maybe the wind moves the bag: Etwas ist im Zelt! If you see nothing at all, you say: Da ist nichts. English works the same way: someone and something, no one and nothing. The German twins even look alike at the start.

cards.title: etwas and nichts
cards.body: etwas = something, anything. nichts = nothing. Both never change their form. In a question etwas means anything: Hast du etwas gegen Mücken? (gegen + accusative = against, for). nichts already says no, like niemand: no nicht. Ben's sentence of the weekend: Ich habe nichts dabei (I have nothing with me).
cards.lead: Now we look closely at the two most useful thing words. With them you can ask for help and say what you do not have.

examples.de: Ich brauche etwas.
examples.en: I need something.

examples.de: Ich habe nichts gegessen.
examples.en: I have eaten nothing.

examples.de: Hast du etwas gegen Mücken?
examples.en: Do you have something against mosquitoes?

deeper.text: After etwas and nichts, an adjective becomes a noun with a capital letter and -es: etwas Neues (something new), nichts Besonderes (nothing special). You hear this every day: Gibt es etwas Neues? Was machst du heute? – Nichts Besonderes. Just recognise these chunks for now; you do not need to build them yourself yet.

example.de: Gibt es etwas Neues?
example.en: Is there anything new?

cards.more: Imagine your pockets. You put your hand in and feel something: Ich habe etwas. You put your hand in and they are empty: Ich habe nichts. That is all. etwas and nichts are like the words Hunger and Durst: one form, always the same, no der or die, no ending. And remember: nichts is already the no. Ich habe nicht nichts is wrong; say Ich habe nichts. One no is enough.

cards.title: alles or alle?
cards.body: alles = everything (things): one big pile, so the verb is singular: Alles ist nass. alle = everyone (people): a group, so the verb is plural: Alle sind nass. Only one letter is different, but the meaning changes. Ask: Do I mean the things or the people?
cards.lead: alle and alles look almost the same. Before Ben's rainy night, we make sure you can tell the people word from the thing word.

examples.de: Alles ist nass.
examples.en: Everything is wet.

examples.de: Alle sind nass.
examples.en: Everyone is wet.

examples.de: Hast du alles? – Ja, alles ist im Rucksack.
examples.en: Have you got everything? – Yes, everything is in the rucksack.

deeper.text: alles lives in many fixed phrases: Alles klar! (all right), Das ist alles (that is all), Alles Gute! (all the best). And a surprise from the north and east of Germany: alle can also mean all gone. Das Wasser ist alle means the water is finished. You may hear this at a festival, but in careful German say: Das Wasser ist leer.

example.de: Das Wasser ist alle.
example.en: The water is all gone.

cards.more: Picture the tent after a night of rain. Look at the floor: the bags, the shoes, the snacks, all one wet pile. That pile is alles, and a pile is one thing: Alles ist nass. Now look at the four friends: Mira, Ben, Leon and Anna, four people, all wet. That is alle, and four people are plural: Alle sind nass. The s at the end of alles is your sign for things.

cards.title: viel and wenig
cards.body: viel = a lot, much. wenig = little, not much. Before a noun without an article, like Wasser or Geld, they have no ending: viel Wasser, wenig Geld. They work like an amount. A very useful festival chunk: Auf dem Festival ist viel los. (A lot is going on.)
cards.lead: We have something, nothing and everything. Now we add the words in between: a lot and a little, for amounts of things.

examples.de: Ich trinke viel Wasser.
examples.en: I drink a lot of water.

examples.de: Wir haben wenig Geld.
examples.en: We have little money.

examples.de: Auf dem Festival ist viel los.
examples.en: A lot is going on at the festival.

deeper.text: viel or viele? Use viel with things you cannot count: viel Wasser, viel Musik, viel Zeit. Use viele with things or people you can count in the plural: viele Leute, viele Zelte. The same with wenig and wenige. So at the festival: Es gibt viele Bands und viel Musik. English makes the same split with much and many.

example.de: Es gibt viele Bands und viel Musik.
example.en: There are many bands and a lot of music.

cards.more: Think of a glass of water and a bag of apples. Water you cannot count, you only say how much: viel Wasser, wenig Wasser. Apples you count, one, two, ten: viele Äpfel, wenige Äpfel. English does the same: much water, many apples. And the chunk Hier ist viel los paints a full, noisy place: lots of people, music, food. The opposite: Hier ist nichts los, nothing is happening.

rows: Auf dem Festival ist viel los.

cards.title: Asking for something politely
cards.body: You can ask in four steps, from simple to very polite: Hast du …? → Kannst du mir … leihen? → Könntest du mir … geben? → Hättest du … für mich? Answers: Ja, klar. or Tut mir leid, ich habe nichts dabei. Ben's phone is empty (leer): he must charge it (aufladen: Er lädt es auf).
cards.lead: You know könnte and hätte from earlier chapters. Now they help Ben: we build a ladder of questions, from simple to very polite.

examples.de: Könntest du mir deine Powerbank leihen?
examples.en: Could you lend me your power bank?

examples.de: Hättest du ein Pflaster für mich?
examples.en: Would you have a plaster for me?

examples.de: Kannst du mir deine Regenjacke leihen?
examples.en: Can you lend me your rain jacket?

deeper.text: Two tiny words make any request softer: vielleicht and kurz. Hättest du vielleicht ein Pflaster für mich? Kann ich kurz deine Powerbank haben? kurz says it is only for a short time, so it is easy to say yes. Germans answer a friend with Klar! or Kein Problem! A no is polite with a reason: Tut mir leid, ich habe nichts dabei.

example.de: Hättest du vielleicht ein Pflaster für mich?
example.en: Would you maybe have a plaster for me?

cards.more: Picture a ladder with four steps. On the lowest step you ask a good friend quickly: Hast du ein Pflaster? Higher up you add mir and leihen: Kannst du mir … leihen? Higher still, the polite könnte: Könntest du …? At the top is the softest form, hätte: Hättest du … für mich? English climbs the same ladder: Got a plaster? Can you lend me …? Could you …? Would you have …?
steps: Hast du ein Pflaster? (simple, for good friends)
Kannst du mir deine Regenjacke leihen?
Könntest du mir deine Powerbank geben?
Hättest du ein Pflaster für mich? (very polite)
Answer: Ja, klar! / Tut mir leid, ich habe nichts dabei.

cards.title: Words for the tent weekend
cards.lead: Many of Ben's things have their own names. This card collects them with their articles and forms, so you know every word before the practice questions.
cards.body: Nouns with article: die Powerbank, das Pflaster, die Regenjacke, das Mückenspray, die Mücke. Two verbs are separable: aufladen (lädt auf) means to charge, and dabeihaben (hat dabei) means to have with you: Ich habe nichts dabei. The small part goes to the end of the sentence.

rows: to charge / to have with you

examples.de: Ich muss mein Handy aufladen.
examples.en: I have to charge my phone.

examples.de: Hast du eine Regenjacke dabei?
examples.en: Do you have a rain jacket with you?

examples.de: Am See gibt es viele Mücken.
examples.en: There are many mosquitoes at the lake.

deeper.text: Mückenspray is a compound: Mücke plus das Spray, and the last word gives the article, so das Mückenspray. In the same way die Regenjacke is Regen plus die Jacke. When dabeihaben stands at the end of a clause, its two parts join again: weil ich nichts dabeihabe. You already know this from separable verbs after weil and in relative clauses.

example.de: Ich weiß nicht, ob Ben ein Pflaster dabeihat.
example.en: I don't know if Ben has a plaster with him.

cards.more: Imagine Ben's rucksack as a little shop. On the shelf lie the things: die Powerbank, das Pflaster, die Regenjacke and das Mückenspray. A mosquito, die Mücke, sits on the edge of the shelf. Ben wants to charge his phone: aufladen. Mira asks: Hast du das dabei? That is dabeihaben, to have it with you. Say the list once aloud and touch each thing in your head: article first, then the word.

cards.title: At the tent: Ben has nothing
cards.body: Ben has forgotten almost everything. Read the six lines: Ben uses nichts, fast nichts (almost nothing) and the polite hättest. Mira helps, but at the end she asks with überhaupt (at all): Ben, hast du überhaupt etwas eingepackt? That means: did you pack anything at all?
cards.lead: Now Ben needs all of today's words at once. In this mini dialogue you see nichts, etwas and the polite questions working together.

examples.de: Ich habe nichts dabei!
examples.en: I have nothing with me!

examples.de: Hast du etwas gegen Mücken?
examples.en: Do you have something against mosquitoes?

examples.de: Ben, hast du überhaupt etwas eingepackt?
examples.en: Ben, did you pack anything at all?

deeper.text: überhaupt makes a question or a no much stronger. Hast du überhaupt etwas eingepackt? sounds a bit shocked: anything at all? With nichts it means nothing at all: Ich habe überhaupt nichts dabei. fast is softer: fast nichts (almost nothing), fast alles (almost everything). These three little words help you say exactly how much.

example.de: Ich habe überhaupt nichts dabei.
example.en: I have nothing at all with me.

cards.more: Imagine a scale for Ben's rucksack. On the left end: überhaupt nichts, totally empty. A little more: fast nichts, maybe a toothbrush. In the middle: etwas. Near the right end: fast alles. On the right end: alles, everything is there. Ben is somewhere near the left, Mira is at the right. Every time you answer a Hast du …? question, you can put yourself on this scale.

rows: Na ja, fast nichts. Hast du etwas gegen Mücken?
Und hättest du ein Pflaster für mich?

lessons.title: Ich habe einen – ich habe keinen: einer, keiner, welche
lessons.goal: Answer 'Do you have a …?' without repeating the noun: einer, eine, eins, welche and keiner, keine, keins.

grammar.topic: einer, eine, eins, welche; keiner, keine, keins
grammar.point: Drop the noun and keep the ein-word as a pronoun with the gender of the noun. Nominative: einer, eine, eins, welche (plural). Accusative: only masculine changes: einen. No: keiner, keine, keins, keine (accusative keinen).
grammar.oneLine: Hast du einen Becher? – Ja, ich habe einen. / Nein, ich habe keinen.

mistake.wrong: Hast du ein Taschentuch? – Nein, ich habe keinen.
mistake.why: The pronoun takes the gender of the noun: das Taschentuch → keins.

terms.meaning: one (as a pronoun, the noun is dropped): masc. einer, fem. eine, neut. eins
none, not one; accusative masc. keinen
some (plural pronoun): Ich habe welche.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'ein Becher' to 'einer'
cards.body: Ben still asks for things all the time: a cup, a tissue, a chair. The others are tired of hearing the same noun twice: Hast du einen Becher? – Ja, ich habe einen Becher. Germans drop the noun and keep only the little ein-word. But it changes a bit: der Becher becomes einer, das Taschentuch becomes eins.
steps: You already know: Ich habe einen Becher. Ich habe keinen Becher. ein / kein + accusative (einen, keinen).
New today: Ich habe einen. Ich habe keinen. Hier ist eins. Da sind welche. The pronoun takes the gender of the noun.
By the end you can: answer Hast du …? without repeating the noun, for der, die, das and plural, with yes and with no.

examples.de: Ich habe einen Becher.
examples.en: I have a cup.
examples.why: You know this: einen + the noun.

examples.de: Ich habe einen.
examples.en: I have one.
examples.why: New today: the noun is gone, einen stays.

cards.more: Think of an echo in the mountains. Ben shouts: Hast du einen Becher? The echo comes back short: … einen! The noun is lost on the way, only the little word comes back. German answers work like this echo. You hear the noun in the question, so you do not need it again in the answer. Your job today: make the echo with the right ending for der, die, das and plural.

cards.title: Don't repeat the noun
cards.body: When the noun is already in the question, the answer can drop it: Hast du einen Becher? – Ja, ich habe einen. The ein-word stays and now stands alone, as a pronoun. It still shows which noun you mean: einer for der, eine for die, eins for das. English uses one for all of them.
cards.lead: In the intro you heard the echo. Now we look at real festival questions and see which little word stays when the noun is gone.

examples.de: Hast du eine Wasserflasche? – Ja, ich habe eine.
examples.en: Do you have a water bottle? – Yes, I have one.

examples.de: Brauchst du ein Taschentuch? – Ja, gib mir eins, bitte.
examples.en: Do you need a tissue? – Yes, give me one, please.

examples.de: Ist hier ein Becher? – Ja, da ist einer.
examples.en: Is there a cup here? – Yes, there is one.

deeper.text: You can also put the pronoun in position 1 to stress it, just like a noun: Einen habe ich noch (I still have one). This is very common in speech when something is almost gone. The verb stays in position 2 and the subject comes after it. The same works with keinen: Keinen habe ich mehr. English often needs a full sentence for this: I've got one left.

example.de: Einen habe ich noch.
example.en: I still have one left.

cards.more: Imagine a shop with an invisible noun. The question puts the word Becher on the table. In your answer you take the noun away, but you leave its little hat on the table: einer or einen. The hat still shows the gender, so everyone knows what you mean. English throws all hats away and just says one: I have one. German keeps the hat: masculine einer or einen, feminine eine, neuter eins.

cards.title: Nominative: einer, eine, eins, welche
cards.body: As the subject (with sein, Da ist …, Hier ist …) the forms are: der → einer, die → eine, das → eins, plural → welche. Look closely: the article ein becomes einer for masculine and eins for neuter. The pronoun shows the gender at the end: -er like der, -s like das.
cards.lead: Now we sort the forms. First the subject forms, which you need after da ist and hier ist. Two of them look different from the article.

examples.de: Da ist einer.
examples.en: There is one. (der Becher)

examples.de: Da ist eine.
examples.en: There is one. (die Isomatte)

examples.de: Da ist eins.
examples.en: There is one. (das Taschentuch)

examples.de: Da sind welche.
examples.en: There are some. (die Snacks)

deeper.text: eins is also the number one: eins, zwei, drei. In careful written German you sometimes read the full form eines instead of eins: Hier ist eines. Both are correct; in speech almost everyone says eins. And when you count things, the pronoun works too: Wie viele Klappstühle sind da? – Nur einer. Only one.

example.de: Wie viele Klappstühle sind da? – Nur einer.
example.en: How many folding chairs are there? – Only one.

cards.more: The article ein is a bit lazy: for der and das it has no ending, so you cannot see the gender. Alone, the pronoun must work harder and show it: einer (like der), eins (like das). So never say Da ist ein. That is half a word: Da ist einer. A trick: listen for the last sound of der, die, das: r, e, s. The pronoun ends the same way: einer, eine, eins.

cards.title: Accusative: einen, eine, eins, welche
cards.body: As the object (with haben, brauchen, nehmen, kaufen) only the masculine form changes, just like the article: einer → einen. Feminine eine, neuter eins and plural welche stay the same. So: Ich habe einen. Ich nehme eine. Ich brauche eins.
cards.lead: After the subject forms, we look at the object forms. Good news: only one form changes, and you already know the change from the article.

examples.de: Ich habe einen.
examples.en: I have one. (der Becher)

examples.de: Ich nehme eine.
examples.en: I'll take one. (die Wasserflasche)

examples.de: Ich brauche eins.
examples.en: I need one. (das Taschentuch)

deeper.text: Remember es gibt? It always takes the accusative, so a masculine noun gets einen: Gibt es hier einen Klappstuhl? – Ja, da hinten gibt es einen. Many learners say einer here, because es gibt feels like da ist. But es gibt works like haben: the thing is the object. Da ist einer and Es gibt einen mean almost the same.

example.de: Ja, da hinten gibt es einen.
example.en: Yes, there is one back there.

cards.more: Think of the accusative as a hand that takes something. When you take a masculine thing, it gets a little extra -n, like a handle: einen. All the others go into your hand unchanged: eine, eins, welche. You know this already from the articles: der → den, ein → einen. The pronoun simply follows the article. So if you can say Ich habe einen Becher, you can say Ich habe einen.

cards.title: The no forms: keiner, keine, keins
cards.body: For no, add k: keiner, keine, keins; plural keine. In the accusative only the masculine changes again: keinen. Hast du einen Kugelschreiber? – Nein, ich habe keinen. Ist hier ein Klappstuhl? – Nein, hier ist keiner. The plural of welche is keine.
cards.lead: You can say yes, I have one. Now we learn to say no, I have none, with the same endings and one extra letter at the start.

examples.de: Hast du einen Kugelschreiber? – Nein, ich habe keinen.
examples.en: Do you have a pen? – No, I don't have one.

examples.de: Ist hier ein Klappstuhl? – Nein, hier ist keiner.
examples.en: Is there a folding chair here? – No, there isn't one.

examples.de: Hast du Snacks? – Nein, ich habe keine.
examples.en: Do you have snacks? – No, I don't have any.

deeper.text: keiner alone, without a noun in the question, often means no one: Keiner hat Zeit is the same as Niemand hat Zeit. In everyday German, keiner is even more common than niemand. Then the verb is singular too. So keiner has two jobs: none of the things, or no person at all. The question before it tells you which one.

example.de: Keiner kommt mit.
example.en: No one is coming along.

cards.more: Imagine a k as a little stop sign in front of the word. einer, eine, eins become keiner, keine, keins. Everything after the stop sign stays the same, even the extra -n in the accusative: einen → keinen. So you only learn one set of endings and use it twice: once for yes, once for no. The only new thing is the plural: yes is welche, no is keine.

cards.title: welche: some (plural)
cards.body: Plural nouns have no ein-article: Hast du Snacks? So for the yes answer German uses welche (some, any): Ja, ich habe welche. With noch it means still some left: Ich habe noch welche. welche is the same as subject and object. The no answer is keine.
cards.lead: einer, eine and eins are always one thing. But what if the question is about many? For plural nouns we need one more word: welche.

examples.de: Hast du Snacks? – Ja, ich habe welche.
examples.en: Do you have snacks? – Yes, I have some.

examples.de: Brauchst du Taschentücher? – Nein, ich habe noch welche.
examples.en: Do you need tissues? – No, I still have some.

examples.de: Sind noch Becher da? – Ja, da sind welche.
examples.en: Are there any cups left? – Yes, there are some.

deeper.text: You know welche as a question word: Welche Mütze brauchst du? (which). Here it is something different, it means some. The question tells you: welch- + noun asks which one; welche alone at the end answers some. And for none left Germans add mehr: Hast du noch welche? – Nein, ich habe keine mehr.

example.de: Hast du noch welche? – Nein, ich habe keine mehr.
example.en: Do you have any left? – No, I don't have any more.

cards.more: Think of a bag of crisps. You cannot answer with one, because the question is about many. English says some: Yes, I have some. German says welche. It is like a hand pointing into the bag: there are some in there. And when the bag is empty, you say keine. That is the whole plural pair: welche for yes, keine for no, and noch welche when there are still some left.

cards.title: The things on the campsite
cards.lead: Before the pronoun questions, we need the things themselves. This card gathers the nouns of the lesson with their plurals, so each answer word has something to point to.
cards.body: Learn each noun with its article, because the article decides einer, eine or eins. Seven camping nouns come up all lesson: der Becher, die Wasserflasche, das Taschentuch, der Snack, der Klappstuhl, die Isomatte and der Müllbeutel. The table shows meaning and plural; a new one is the rubbish bag.

examples.de: Der Müllbeutel ist voll.
examples.en: The rubbish bag is full.

examples.de: Leon bringt zwei Klappstühle mit.
examples.en: Leon brings two folding chairs.

examples.de: Ohne Isomatte ist der Boden kalt.
examples.en: Without a sleeping mat the ground is cold.

deeper.text: Look at the plurals. der Becher and der Müllbeutel do not change: die Becher, die Müllbeutel. Many nouns ending in -er or -el stay the same. But der Klappstuhl and das Taschentuch get an umlaut: die Klappstühle, die Taschentücher. So the plural is part of the word. Learn der Becher, die Becher as one chunk, and then welche is easy to use.

example.de: Wir haben zwei Becher und drei Klappstühle.
example.en: We have two cups and three folding chairs.

cards.more: Think of a camping box with seven things in it. Each thing has a label with its article: der Becher, die Wasserflasche, das Taschentuch. When someone asks Hast du …?, you look at the label and you know the answer word: einen, eine or eins. A label without the article is useless, like a box without a lid. So when you meet a new camping word, say it with der, die or das, and say its plural once.

cards.title: Three steps and a festival dialogue
cards.body: Find the form in three steps. Then read Ben and Anna at the festival. Notice: Anna answers with the gender of each noun, and with yes or no.
cards.lead: Now you have all the forms. These three steps help you choose the right one quickly, and the dialogue shows them in a real conversation.

examples.de: Hast du eine Isomatte? – Ja, hier ist eine.
examples.en: Do you have a sleeping mat? – Yes, here is one.

examples.de: Brauchst du einen Müllbeutel? – Ja, gib mir einen, bitte.
examples.en: Do you need a rubbish bag? – Yes, give me one, please.

examples.de: Hast du ein Taschentuch? – Nein, ich habe keins.
examples.en: Do you have a tissue? – No, I don't have one.

deeper.text: eins or es? eins means any one: Hast du ein Taschentuch? – Hier ist eins. es means the one we both know: Wo ist mein Taschentuch? – Hier ist es. The same for einer or er: Wo ist mein Becher? – Da ist er. So the question decides: ein-word in the question, eins in the answer; mein- or der-word in the question, es or er.

example.de: Wo ist mein Taschentuch? – Hier ist es.
example.en: Where is my tissue? – Here it is.

cards.more: Use the steps like a recipe. First look at the noun: der, die, das or plural? Then look at the verb: is the thing the subject (Da ist …) or the object (Ich habe …)? Last: yes or no? Masculine object yes: einen. Neuter no: keins. Plural yes: welche. After a few days you will not need the recipe any more, but at the start it stops you from always saying einen.
steps: 1 Which noun? der, die, das or plural?
2 Subject (Da ist …, Hier ist …) → nominative; object (haben, brauchen, nehmen) → accusative.
3 Yes → einer / einen / eine / eins / welche. No → keiner / keinen / keine / keins / keine.
Ben: Hast du eine Isomatte? – Anna: Ja, hier ist eine.
Ben: Und ein Taschentuch? – Anna: Nein, ich habe keins. Aber Leon hat welche.

lessons.title: Das ist die Band, die …: relative clauses (nominative)
lessons.goal: Talk about music and describe a person or a thing with a relative clause: der, die, das, die + verb at the end.

grammar.topic: relative clauses in the nominative: der, die, das, die
grammar.point: Join two sentences about the same noun: replace the second noun with der (m), die (f), das (n) or die (pl), put a comma before it and send the verb to the end, as after weil. The pronoun copies the gender of its noun. das (relative) points back to a noun; dass follows sagen, glauben, finden.
grammar.oneLine: Das ist der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt.

mistake.wrong: Das ist der Sänger, der kommt aus Hamburg.
mistake.right: Das ist der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt.
mistake.why: In the relative clause the verb goes to the end.

terms.meaning: a clause after a comma that describes a noun: …, der aus Hamburg kommt
der / die / das / die: points back to the noun and copies its gender
das points back to a neuter noun; dass follows sagen, glauben, finden

cards.title: Before we start: from '…, weil die Band gut spielt' to '…, die gut spielt'
cards.body: Leon has a new playlist and wants to show Mira every song. He keeps using two short sentences: Das ist ein Sänger. Er kommt aus Hamburg. Germans join the two with a little word that points back to the noun. And you already know the hard part: the verb goes to the end, like after weil.
steps: You already know: Ich mag die Band, weil sie gut spielt. With weil and dass the verb goes to the end.
New today: Das ist der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt. der, die, das, die point back to a noun, and the verb goes to the end.
By the end you can: talk about music, join two sentences into one and describe a singer, a song or a band.

examples.de: Das ist ein Sänger. Er kommt aus Hamburg.
examples.en: That's a singer. He comes from Hamburg.
examples.why: You know this: two short sentences.

examples.de: Das ist der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt.
examples.en: That's the singer who comes from Hamburg.
examples.why: New today: one sentence, der points back, kommt goes to the end.

cards.more: Think of a label on a jar. The jar is the noun: der Sänger. The label says something about it: comes from Hamburg. In German you stick the label on with a comma and the little word der, which means this one here. Then the verb of the label goes to the end, as you know from weil. Today you learn to make these labels for people, songs and bands.

cards.title: Talking about music
cards.body: Before we join sentences, we need words for music. Ask Was hörst du gern? and answer with Ich höre gern … plus the music: Rock, Jazz, Klassik, Pop. die Musikrichtung is the genre. For a favourite, say am liebsten. Instruments: das Schlagzeug, die Geige, das Klavier, die Gitarre.
cards.lead: The intro showed Leon's playlist. First we collect the music words he needs: genres, instruments and the question Was hörst du gern?

examples.de: Was hörst du gern?
examples.en: What do you like listening to?

examples.de: Ich höre gern Rock und Jazz.
examples.en: I like listening to rock and jazz.

examples.de: Meine Musikrichtung ist Pop.
examples.en: My music genre is pop.

examples.de: Frau Weber hört am liebsten Klassik.
examples.en: Frau Weber likes classical music best.

deeper.text: Musik hören means you listen; Musik machen means you play yourself. With instruments German uses spielen and no article: Ich spiele Geige. English needs the: I play the violin. Genres also have no article in these sentences: Ich höre gern Jazz, Ich mag Klassik. die Klassik means classical music as a whole, so you never say eine Klassik.

example.de: Ich spiele Gitarre, aber nicht Geige.
example.en: I play the guitar, but not the violin.

cards.more: Think of a music shop with two walls. On one wall hang the instruments: das Schlagzeug, die Geige, das Klavier, die Gitarre. On the other wall the shelves have labels: Rock, Jazz, Klassik, Pop. Each label is a Musikrichtung. When a friend asks Was hörst du gern?, walk to a shelf and read its label. When they ask Was spielst du?, walk to the instruments and name one, without der or die.

cards.title: Two sentences become one
cards.body: Two sentences often talk about the same noun: Das ist der Sänger. Der Sänger kommt aus Hamburg. German joins them. Replace the second der Sänger with der, put a comma before it and send the verb to the end. This little der is a relative pronoun: it points back to the noun.
cards.lead: Now you have the music words. Here is the main trick of today: two short sentences about one person become one longer sentence.

examples.de: Das ist der Sänger. Der Sänger kommt aus Hamburg.
examples.en: That's the singer. The singer comes from Hamburg.

examples.de: Das ist der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt.
examples.en: That's the singer who comes from Hamburg.

examples.de: Das ist die Geige. Die Geige ist sehr alt.
examples.en: That's the violin. The violin is very old.

examples.de: Das ist die Geige, die sehr alt ist.
examples.en: That's the violin that is very old.

deeper.text: English chooses by meaning: who for people, which or that for things. German does not care whether it is a person or a thing. It only asks about the gender of the noun: der Sänger, der …; der Song, der …. And English can sometimes drop the word: the song I like. German never can. The pronoun and the comma must always be there.

example.de: Das ist der Song, der mir gefällt.
example.en: That's the song I like (that pleases me).

cards.more: Imagine two Lego bricks with the same name on top: der Sänger. You can click them together, but only if one brick gives its name away. The second brick loses its noun and keeps just der, a little hook. The hook clicks onto the first noun with a comma. Inside the new brick the verb slides to the very end, like after weil. Two bricks, one sentence, and the noun is never said twice.
steps: 1 Same noun twice? Replace the second one with der / die / das / die.
2 Put a comma before the pronoun.
3 Send the verb to the end: …, der aus Hamburg kommt.

cards.title: der, die, das, die: like the article
cards.body: The relative pronoun copies the gender of its noun: masculine der, feminine die, neuter das, plural die. It looks exactly like the article you learn with the noun. So learn every noun with der, die or das, and the pronoun comes for free: die Sängerin, die …; das Lied, das ….
cards.lead: Card 2 used der for der Sänger. But the pronoun is not always der: it changes with the noun. Here are all four forms.

examples.de: Das ist die Sängerin, die so schön singt.
examples.en: That's the singer who sings so beautifully.

examples.de: Das ist das Lied, das gerade läuft.
examples.en: That's the song that is playing right now.

examples.de: Das sind die Musiker, die heute spielen.
examples.en: Those are the musicians who are playing today.

deeper.text: The pronoun follows the grammar of the noun, not the person. das Mädchen is neuter, so: das Mädchen, das singt. die Band is feminine, even when five men play in it: die Band, die aus Hamburg kommt. With ein, kein or mein before the noun you still use der, die or das: ein Song, der …; meine Band, die …. Only the noun's gender counts.

example.de: Das ist meine Band, die in Kiel spielt.
example.en: That's my band that plays in Kiel.

cards.more: Think of the pronoun as the noun's shadow. A shadow has the same shape as the thing: der Sänger casts der, die Sängerin casts die, das Lied casts das. Many learners always say der, because it feels like English who. But die Sängerin, der singt is wrong: the shadow has the wrong shape. Right is die Sängerin, die singt. Look back at the noun, copy its article, and you are done.

cards.title: The verb goes to the end
cards.body: Inside the relative clause the conjugated verb stands at the very end, exactly as after weil or dass. The main sentence keeps its verb in position 2. So the sentence has two verbs: hat near the start, ist at the end: Leon hat eine Gitarre, die sehr alt ist.
cards.lead: You know the four pronouns. Now look at the other end of the relative clause: where its verb goes, and why it feels like weil.

examples.de: Ich mag Musik, die laut ist.
examples.en: I like music that is loud.

examples.de: Leon hat eine Gitarre, die sehr alt ist.
examples.en: Leon has a guitar that is very old.

examples.de: Ich kenne einen Song, der nur zwei Minuten dauert.
examples.en: I know a song that lasts only two minutes.

deeper.text: In today's clauses the pronoun is the subject of its own clause. So the verb at the end agrees with it, and the pronoun agrees with the noun: der Song … dauert, but die Songs … dauern. Plural noun, plural verb. Check it like a mini sentence: Die Songs dauern nur zwei Minuten → Songs, die nur zwei Minuten dauern.

example.de: Ich kenne Songs, die nur zwei Minuten dauern.
example.en: I know songs that last only two minutes.

cards.more: Picture a train. The main sentence is the engine, with its verb in the second wagon. After the comma a new little train starts, and the pronoun is its engine. In this little train the verb is the last wagon, the one that arrives at the station last. English keeps the verb close: the guitar that is old. German makes you wait: die Gitarre, die sehr alt … ist. Wait for it, then say it.

cards.title: das or dass?
cards.body: They sound the same. Relative das points back to a neuter noun: das Album, das neu ist. dass comes after verbs like sagen, glauben, finden and starts a new statement. Quick test: can you say welches instead? Then write das. If welches makes no sense, write dass.
cards.lead: The neuter pronoun das sounds just like dass, which you know from A2. This card gives you a quick test to tell them apart.

examples.de: Das ist ein Hit, der überall läuft.
examples.en: That's a hit that is playing everywhere.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass der Hit neu ist.
examples.en: I think that the hit is new.

examples.de: Das ist das Album, das am besten ist.
examples.en: That's the album that is the best.

deeper.text: welches is an old relative pronoun. You see it in some books, but in speech Germans use das. That is why the test works: das Album, welches neu ist sounds old, but correct, so das is right. Ich glaube, welches der Hit neu ist makes no sense, so it must be dass. Look left: a neuter noun before the comma means das; sagen or glauben means dass.

example.de: Leon sagt, dass das Lied neu ist.
example.en: Leon says that the song is new.

cards.more: Think of das as a finger pointing back at a thing: das Lied, das … – the finger touches the song. dass is a door. After sagen or glauben you open the door, and a whole new statement walks in: Ich glaube, dass … English hides the difference, because that does both jobs: the song that plays, I think that it plays. In German the spelling shows the job: one s points back, two s open a door.

cards.title: Words for songs and singers
cards.lead: You have met many music words in the lessons. This card puts the last ones in one place, with their articles and plurals, because the article decides which pronoun comes after the comma.
cards.body: die Melodie is the tune you hum. der Song and der Hit are everyday words from English: a Hit is a very popular song. The singers: der Sänger, die Sängerin, from singen. For music styles you use der Jazz and die Klassik, but without an article in sentences: Ich höre gern Jazz. Learn the article with each noun.

examples.de: Die Melodie ist schön.
examples.en: The melody is beautiful.

examples.de: Das ist ein Hit, der überall läuft.
examples.en: That's a hit that is playing everywhere.

examples.de: Mira kennt die Melodie.
examples.en: Mira knows the tune.

deeper.text: Song and Hit come from English, but in German they have an article: der Song, der Hit. The German word for song, das Lied, is neuter. So you say das Lied, das läuft, but der Song, der läuft. That is why you must learn the article with the word: it decides the relative pronoun. A singer is a Sänger or a Sängerin, depending on gender.

example.de: Das ist ein Lied, das gerade läuft.
example.en: That's a song that is playing right now.

cards.more: Imagine a radio. Out of the speaker comes die Melodie, the tune you hum in the shower. Then a voice joins: it is der Sänger or die Sängerin, and the song is a Hit if everybody knows it. At the end the presenter says: Das war ein Song, der gerade überall läuft. Radio words always come with an article, because the next part of the sentence needs der, die or das after the comma, and you can only choose it if you know the gender.

cards.title: Leon shows Mira his playlist
cards.body: Read the six lines. Each relative clause describes a song, a singer or a band. Find the pronoun after each comma, look back at its noun and find the verb at the end. Two new chunks: Hör mal! (Listen!) and gerade (right now).
cards.lead: Now all the pieces come together. Leon shows Mira the songs on his phone, and every description is a relative clause.

examples.de: Hör mal! Das ist der Song, der gerade überall läuft.
examples.en: Listen! That's the song that's playing everywhere right now.

examples.de: Eine Sängerin, die aus Wien kommt.
examples.en: A singer who comes from Vienna.

examples.de: Das ist die Band, die nächsten Monat in Kiel spielt.
examples.en: That's the band that plays in Kiel next month.

deeper.text: Gute Unterhaltung! means Enjoy the show! You hear it before a concert, a film or a show on TV. die Unterhaltung is entertainment, but also a conversation. With friends Germans more often say Viel Spaß!. Gute Unterhaltung! sounds a bit more like a host talking to the audience, so Mira says it with a smile.

example.de: Viel Spaß beim Konzert!
example.en: Have fun at the concert!

cards.more: Read the dialogue like a guided tour of Leon's phone. Each time he shows something, he first names it: der Song, eine Sängerin, die Band. Then, after a comma, he adds a little label, the relative clause, which says what is special about it. Mira answers with short reactions. When you talk about music, do the same: name the thing, then add a label with der, die or das and the verb at the end.
steps: Leon: Hör mal! Das ist der Song, der gerade überall läuft.
Mira: Wer singt das?
Leon: Eine Sängerin, die aus Wien kommt.
Mira: Die Stimme ist toll! (die Stimme = the voice)
Leon: Und das ist die Band, die nächsten Monat in Kiel spielt.
Mira: Gute Unterhaltung!

lessons.title: Die Band, die heute spielt, …: presenting a band
lessons.goal: Present a musician or a band with several relative clauses, also with modal verbs, Perfekt and separable verbs, and with the clause in the middle.

grammar.topic: relative clauses: modal, Perfekt and separable verbs; clause in the middle
grammar.point: In the relative clause every verb goes to the end. Modal: infinitive + modal (…, der singen kann). Perfekt: participle + hat/ist (…, die das Album gemacht hat). Separable verbs join up (…, die heute auftritt). A clause in the middle has a comma on both sides, then the main verb: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg.
grammar.oneLine: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg.

mistake.wrong: Die Band, die heute spielt kommt aus Hamburg.
mistake.right: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg.
mistake.why: A relative clause in the middle needs a comma on both sides; then the main verb follows.

terms.meaning: Noun, relative clause, comma, main verb: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt …
infinitive + modal (singen kann) or participle + hat/ist (gemacht hat)

terms.term: separable verb in a relative clause
terms.meaning: the parts join again at the end: auftritt, anfängt

cards.title: Before we start: from one relative clause to a band portrait
cards.body: Leon wants to write about his favourite band, Die Nachteulen, for the WG blog. One relative clause per sentence is not enough: he needs can, has done and performs, and sometimes the clause must stand in the middle of the sentence. Today you learn where every verb goes, so a whole band portrait sounds natural.
steps: You already know: Das ist die Band, die in Kiel spielt. der, die, das, die + verb at the end.
New today: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg. Also: …, der singen kann / …, die das Album gemacht hat / …, die heute auftritt.
By the end you can: present a musician or a band in five or six sentences with several relative clauses.

examples.de: Das ist die Band, die in Kiel spielt.
examples.en: That's the band that plays in Kiel.
examples.why: You know this from lesson 4.

examples.de: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg.
examples.en: The band that's playing today comes from Hamburg.
examples.why: New today: the relative clause sits in the middle.

cards.more: Think of a sandwich. In lesson 4 the relative clause was always the last slice: Das ist die Band, die in Kiel spielt. Today you also put it in the middle: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg. The bread is the main sentence, the filling is the relative clause, and the commas hold it together on both sides. Then you add verbs with two parts.

cards.title: Die Nachteulen: two sentences become one
cards.body: A quick review with the WG's favourite band, Die Nachteulen (the night owls). Same noun twice? Replace the second with der, die, das or die, add a comma and send the verb to the end. Watch the gender: die Band, but der Schlagzeuger and die Sängerin.
cards.lead: In the intro you saw the plan for today. First we warm up with lesson 4: two sentences about Die Nachteulen become one.

examples.de: Die Nachteulen sind eine Band, die aus Hamburg kommt.
examples.en: Die Nachteulen are a band that comes from Hamburg.

examples.de: Die Sängerin ist eine Frau, die auch Gitarre spielt.
examples.en: The singer is a woman who also plays the guitar.

examples.de: Der Schlagzeuger ist ein Musiker, der sehr gut ist.
examples.en: The drummer is a musician who is very good.

deeper.text: Look at the first example: Die Nachteulen sind (plural), but eine Band, die … kommt (singular). The pronoun points to the noun right before the comma, eine Band, not to the name at the start. So the verb at the end is singular. Band names are often plural in German, like Die Nachteulen, but die Band stays feminine singular.

example.de: Die Nachteulen sind Musiker, die aus Hamburg kommen.
example.en: Die Nachteulen are musicians who come from Hamburg.

cards.more: Imagine a pointing finger after each comma. It always points at the noun just before it, never further back. In Die Nachteulen sind eine Band, die aus Hamburg kommt, the finger touches eine Band: one band, so kommt. Change the noun to Musiker and the finger touches a group: die … kommen. English does the same with who and which, but you never see the difference in the verb. In German you hear it.

rows: Das ist eine Band. Die Band kommt aus Hamburg.
Das ist eine Band, die aus Hamburg kommt.
Er ist ein Musiker. Der Musiker ist sehr gut.
Er ist ein Musiker, der sehr gut ist.
Das sind Musiker. Die Musiker kommen aus Hamburg.
Das sind Musiker, die aus Hamburg kommen.

cards.title: A modal verb in the relative clause
cards.body: With a modal verb like können or wollen, the infinitive and the modal both go to the end. The modal is the very last word: …, der sehr hoch singen kann. It is the same order you know from weil: weil er singen kann.
cards.lead: The review had one verb in each clause. Now we add a second verb: a modal like können or wollen. Where do both verbs go?

examples.de: Das ist ein Sänger, der sehr hoch singen kann.
examples.en: That's a singer who can sing very high.

examples.de: Ich suche eine Band, die auf dem Festival spielen will.
examples.en: I'm looking for a band that wants to play at the festival.

examples.de: Leon ist ein Musiker, der gut Gitarre spielen kann.
examples.en: Leon is a musician who can play the guitar well.

deeper.text: Compare with a normal sentence: Der Sänger kann sehr hoch singen. There kann is in position 2 and singen at the end. In the relative clause the modal moves too: it jumps from position 2 to behind singen. So the two verbs simply swap places. This is the same in every clause with the verb at the end: weil, dass, wenn and now der, die, das.

example.de: Der Sänger kann sehr hoch singen.
example.en: The singer can sing very high.

cards.more: Think of a queue at the concert. In a normal sentence the modal stands at the front of the queue and the infinitive waits at the back. In the relative clause the modal is late: it walks past everybody and stands behind the infinitive, at the very end. So you get singen kann, spielen will, auftreten muss. English keeps can before sing; German puts it after. Say it slowly a few times: der hoch singen kann.

rows: Die Band will auf dem Festival spielen.
…, die auf dem Festival spielen will.

cards.title: Perfekt in the relative clause
cards.body: In the Perfekt the participle and hat or ist go to the end, and hat or ist is the last word: …, die das Album gemacht hat. Verbs of movement keep ist: …, der aus Köln gekommen ist. For a state today, simply use the present: …, das sehr erfolgreich ist.
cards.lead: Modal verbs go behind the infinitive. The Perfekt works the same way: the participle first, then hat or ist at the very end.

examples.de: Das ist die Band, die das Album gemacht hat.
examples.en: That's the band that made the album.

examples.de: Das ist der Musiker, der aus Köln gekommen ist.
examples.en: That's the musician who came from Cologne.

examples.de: Die Band hat ein Album, das sehr erfolgreich ist.
examples.en: The band has an album that is very successful.

deeper.text: In speech Germans use the Perfekt for the past, also in relative clauses. So the sentence can end with two forms of haben: Die Band, die das Album gemacht hat, hat viele Fans. The first hat closes the relative clause, the second is the main verb. It looks strange, but it is correct, and the commas show where each part ends.

example.de: Die Band, die das Album gemacht hat, hat viele Fans.
example.en: The band that made the album has many fans.

cards.more: Picture a suitcase with two locks at the end. The participle gemacht is the first lock, hat is the second, and you always close them in this order: gemacht hat, gekommen ist. If you put hat first, the suitcase stays open. English says the band that has made the album, with has early. German waits and closes everything at the end. A quick check: is the last word hat or ist? Then the Perfekt clause is closed.
steps: 1 Perfekt sentence: Die Band hat das Album gemacht.
2 Pronoun instead of the noun: …, die …
3 Participle, then hat or ist at the end: …, die das Album gemacht hat.

cards.title: Separable verbs join up again
cards.body: Separable verbs split in a normal sentence: Die Band tritt heute auf. In the relative clause the verb goes to the end, so the two parts join again into one word: …, die heute auftritt. auftreten means to perform on stage; der Auftritt is the performance or gig.
cards.lead: Modal and Perfekt put two words at the end. A separable verb does the opposite: its two parts come together again as one word.

examples.de: Die Band tritt heute auf.
examples.en: The band performs today.

examples.de: Das ist die Band, die heute auftritt.
examples.en: That's the band that performs today.

examples.de: Das ist die Sängerin, die morgen in Kiel auftritt.
examples.en: That's the singer who performs in Kiel tomorrow.

deeper.text: The same happens with every separable verb you know: anfangen, mitkommen, aufladen. Der Auftritt, der um acht anfängt. Ein Freund, der mitkommt. Only with a modal do they stay as one word before the modal: …, die heute auftreten will. In the Perfekt the ge sits inside: aufgetreten. So listen for the small word at the end; it tells you which verb it is.

example.de: Das ist der Auftritt, der um acht anfängt.
example.en: That's the gig that starts at eight.

cards.more: Think of a magnet split into two halves. In a normal sentence the verb tritt stands in position 2 and its little half auf waits at the end. In the relative clause the verb moves to the end too, so the halves meet and click: auftritt. Many learners leave them apart: die Sängerin, die tritt morgen auf. That is wrong. Right is die Sängerin, die morgen auftritt: one word, last place.

rows: Das Konzert fängt um acht an.

cards.title: A relative clause in the middle
cards.body: The relative clause can describe the subject at the start. Then it sits in the middle, with a comma on both sides, and the main verb follows straight after the second comma. You see verb, comma, verb: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg.
cards.lead: So far the relative clause came at the end. Now the noun is at the start, so the clause moves into the middle of the sentence.

examples.de: Die Band, die heute spielt, kommt aus Hamburg.
examples.en: The band that's playing today comes from Hamburg.

examples.de: Der Song, der jetzt läuft, ist neu.
examples.en: The song that's playing now is new.

examples.de: Die Musiker, die hier auftreten, sind sehr jung.
examples.en: The musicians who perform here are very young.

deeper.text: The whole first part, Die Band, die heute spielt, counts as position 1. That is why the main verb comes right after it, in position 2. In English you hear no break, but in German you must write the second comma, and in speech you make a tiny pause there. Without it the two verbs, spielt kommt, run into each other.

example.de: Die Sängerin, die die Texte schreibt, singt auch.
example.en: The singer who writes the lyrics also sings.

cards.more: Picture a parcel with a ribbon around it. The noun Die Band is the parcel. The relative clause is the ribbon, tied on with a comma at each side: , die heute spielt, . The parcel and its ribbon are one thing, so they take position 1 together. Then the main verb comes, as always, in position 2: kommt. If you forget the second comma, the ribbon is open and the reader does not know where the main sentence starts again.

cards.title: Words for a band portrait
cards.lead: Leon's portrait needs a few more words: the woman who plays, the verb to found, and the things on stage. Here they are with their articles and forms.
cards.body: Nouns: die Musikerin is the woman who plays music; das Mikrofon is what she sings into; der Text means the lyrics. Verb: gründen means to found or start a band: Die Musiker haben die Band gegründet. Adjective: erfolgreich means successful: Das Album ist sehr erfolgreich. Learn the plural with each noun.

examples.de: Die Musikerin singt ins Mikrofon.
examples.en: The musician sings into the microphone.

examples.de: Die Musiker haben die Band 2019 gegründet.
examples.en: The musicians founded the band in 2019.

examples.de: Das Album ist sehr erfolgreich.
examples.en: The album is very successful.

deeper.text: Because the stem of gründen ends in d, the participle ends in -et: gegründet, like gearbeitet. In a relative clause you meet it at the end: …, die die Musiker gegründet haben. Also notice that die Musikerin is the feminine form of der Musiker: you add -in. Most job words work like that, and the plural adds -nen: die Musikerinnen.

example.de: Das ist die Band, die die Musiker 2019 gegründet haben.
example.en: That's the band the musicians founded in 2019.

cards.more: Think of Leon's band poster. On the poster there is a Musikerin with a Mikrofon in her hand. Under her name stands the band's story: Die Nachteulen haben die Band 2019 gegründet. The album did well, so Leon writes erfolgreich. The lyrics, die Texte, are printed on the back. Take each word in turn and make one short sentence about the Nachteulen. Say it aloud, with the article and the Perfekt where it fits.

cards.title: Present a band
cards.body: Use five questions as a plan: Name? Woher? Wer spielt was? Musikrichtung? Warum gut? Answer each with one sentence, and use relative clauses for details. Then read Leon's portrait of Die Nachteulen. New chunk: eine tolle Stimme haben (to have a great voice).
cards.lead: Now you can put every kind of verb at the end. Here is a plan for a whole band portrait, and Leon's model text.

examples.de: Die Nachteulen sind eine Band, die aus Hamburg kommt.
examples.en: Die Nachteulen are a band that comes from Hamburg.

examples.de: Die Musiker haben die Band 2019 gegründet.
examples.en: The musicians founded the band in 2019.

examples.de: Die Sängerin, die auch die Texte schreibt, hat eine tolle Stimme.
examples.en: The singer, who also writes the lyrics, has a great voice.

deeper.text: In a portrait, two short sentences in a row are good; four in a row sound like a list. One relative clause per two or three sentences is natural. Germans also like ending with a personal opinion: Ich mag die Band, weil … or Ich finde, dass …. So you mix all your verb-at-the-end tools: der/die/das, weil and dass. That mix makes a text sound like real German.

example.de: Ich finde, dass die Texte sehr gut sind.
example.en: I think that the lyrics are very good.

cards.more: Think of a band poster. At the top the big name, then a small line: from Hamburg. Under it the photos of the musicians, each with a little note: the singer who writes the lyrics, the drummer who plays very fast. At the bottom a quote from a fan. Your text works like this poster: name and city first, then the people with relative clauses as notes, and your own opinion at the end.
steps: 1 Name: Die Nachteulen sind eine Band, die aus Hamburg kommt.
2 Woher? Seit wann? Die Musiker haben die Band 2019 gegründet.
3 Wer spielt was? Die Sängerin, die auch die Texte schreibt, hat eine tolle Stimme. Der Schlagzeuger ist ein Musiker, der sehr schnell spielen kann.
4 Musikrichtung: Ihre Musikrichtung ist Rock.
5 Warum gut? Ich mag die Band, weil ihre Auftritte immer laut und lustig sind.
