lessons.title: Wie bitte? Wann?: echo questions and a newspaper report
lessons.goal: Ask back when you didn't understand (echo questions, polite Rückfragen) and get exact information about people and events, for example from a short newspaper report.

grammar.topic: echo questions and Rückfragen; Wer ist …, der/die …?
grammar.point: To ask back, repeat only the question word that fits the missing piece (Wann? Wo genau? Woher? Wer?) with a rising melody and stress on the question word. Politer: Wie bitte? / Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? / Habe ich das richtig verstanden: …? For people: Wer ist die Frau, die …?
grammar.oneLine: Die Band spielt um zehn. – Wann? / Um wie viel Uhr?

mistake.wrong: Die Band spielt um zehn. – Wann spielt?
mistake.right: Die Band spielt um zehn. – Wann spielt die Band?
mistake.why: An echo question is only the question word (Wann?, Um wie viel Uhr?) or the whole question; never question word + verb alone.

terms.meaning: asking back with only the question word: Wann? Wo genau? (voice goes up)
a question to check information: Wie bitte? Können Sie das wiederholen?
Wer? Was? Wann? Wo? Warum? find the key facts

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Wann spielt die Band?' to 'Wann bitte?'
cards.body: At a festival it is loud. You hear half a sentence: Die Band spielt um … zehn? Instead of a long question, Germans repeat just the question word with a rising voice: Wann? Today you learn these echo questions, polite Rückfragen and how to read a short report.
steps: You already know: W-questions (Wann spielt die Band? Wo ist das Konzert?) and stress on the important word (ch11).
New today: Die Band spielt um zehn. – Um wie viel Uhr? / Wann bitte? Echo questions go up at the end.
By the end you can: ask back when you didn't understand, check information politely and answer W-questions about a short report.

examples.de: Wann spielt die Band?
examples.en: When does the band play?
examples.why: You know this: a normal W-question.

examples.de: Die Band spielt um zehn. – Wann bitte?
examples.en: The band plays at ten. – When, sorry?
examples.why: New today: only the question word, to ask back.

cards.more: Think of a mountain echo again, but this time it is a question. Someone says: Das Konzert ist am Freitag. You missed one word, so you send back only the missing piece: Wann? Your voice goes up like a question mark. The other person repeats the piece you need. Short, quick and friendly, and you do not have to build a whole new sentence in the noise.

cards.title: Echo question: repeat the question word
cards.body: When you miss one piece of information, ask back with the matching question word only: time → Wann?, place → Wo? or Wo genau?, origin → Woher?, person → Wer? The other person then repeats that piece. Choose the word that fits the missing information.
cards.lead: The intro showed the idea. Now we practise which question word fits which missing piece: time, place, origin or person.

examples.de: Das Konzert ist am Freitag. – Wann?
examples.en: The concert is on Friday. – When?

examples.de: Die Sängerin kommt aus Wien. – Woher?
examples.en: The singer comes from Vienna. – Where from?

examples.de: Wir treffen uns vor der Bühne. – Wo genau?
examples.en: We'll meet in front of the stage. – Where exactly?

deeper.text: You can also repeat the sentence and put the question word where the missing piece was: Das Konzert ist wann? or Die Sängerin kommt woher? This sounds surprised, and it is very common in speech. It keeps the normal word order and only swaps the piece. In writing and in polite talk the short form or a full question is safer.

example.de: Das Konzert ist wann?
example.en: The concert is when?

cards.more: Imagine a form with one empty box. Your friend fills in the form out loud, but one box stays empty because of the noise. You do not ask for the whole form again; you only point at the empty box: Wann? Wo? Wer? English does the same: When? Where? But English often adds sorry. In German, the short word alone is fine with friends; with Frau Weber you add bitte or Entschuldigung.

cards.title: The melody goes up
cards.body: A normal W-question goes down at the end ↘: Wann spielt die Band? An echo question goes up ↗, because you ask back: Wann? Put the stress on the question word (stress WANN, WO, WER) and let your voice rise. The rising melody shows: please repeat that.
cards.lead: You know which word to use. Now the sound: an echo question has its own melody, and that melody tells the other person you are asking back.

examples.de: Wann spielt die Band?
examples.en: When does the band play? (↘ voice goes down)

examples.de: Die Band spielt um zehn. – Wann?
examples.en: The band plays at ten. – When? (↗ stress WANN, voice goes up)

examples.de: Leon kommt aus Kiel. – Woher?
examples.en: Leon comes from Kiel. – Where from? (↗ stress HER)

deeper.text: The melody also shows your feeling. A quick, high Wann? means: I didn't hear you. A long, very high Wie bitte? with big eyes means: I can't believe it! Germans use this for surprise: Das Ticket kostet hundert Euro. – Wie viel? So the same words can be a real question or a little shock, and your voice decides which one.

example.de: Das Ticket kostet hundert Euro. – Wie viel?
example.en: The ticket costs a hundred euros. – How much? (↗ surprised)

cards.more: Picture your voice as a ball. In a normal question you throw the ball, and it falls down at the end: Wann spielt die Band? ↘. In an echo question you throw it back up into the air: Wann? ↗. The other person has to catch it and answer. English works in a similar way: When? with a rising voice. So you can use your English feeling here, just with German words, and stress the question word.
steps: Normal W-question: Wann spielt die Band? ↘ (voice down)
Echo question: Wann? ↗ (stress WANN, voice up)
Echo question: Wo genau? ↗ (stress GE in genau)
Surprise: Wie viel? ↗↗ (very high)

cards.title: Asking back politely
cards.body: With friends one word is fine. With Frau Weber or on the phone, be more polite. There is a ladder from short to very polite: Wie bitte? → Entschuldigung, wann genau? → Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? → Habe ich das richtig verstanden: am Samstag?
cards.lead: Echo questions are short and quick. But with older people like Frau Weber, or in a shop, you need longer and more polite ways to ask back.

examples.de: Wie bitte?
examples.en: Sorry? / Pardon?

examples.de: Entschuldigung, wann genau?
examples.en: Excuse me, when exactly?

examples.de: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?
examples.en: Could you repeat that, please?

examples.de: Habe ich das richtig verstanden? Am Samstag?
examples.en: Did I understand that correctly? On Saturday?

deeper.text: Was? alone sounds rude to many Germans, a bit like What? in English. Parents tell children: Nicht Was?, sondern Wie bitte? So with strangers say Wie bitte? Habe ich das richtig verstanden? is great for checking: you repeat the information yourself, and the other person only has to say ja or nein. On the phone that saves time.

example.de: Habe ich das richtig verstanden? Um acht? – Ja, genau.
example.en: Did I get that right? At eight? – Yes, exactly.

cards.more: Think of a staircase. The bottom step is Wie bitte?: quick and always fine. One step higher you add the question word: Entschuldigung, wann genau? Higher still you ask for a repeat: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? On the top step you check it yourself: Habe ich das richtig verstanden: am Samstag? The more important the information, a train time or a date, the higher you climb.

rows: Habe ich das richtig verstanden: am Samstag?

cards.title: Reading a newspaper report
cards.body: A short report (die Meldung) answers five W-questions: Wer? Was? Wann? Wo? Warum? The headline (die Schlagzeile) gives the main point. Read it once quickly, then look for one answer for each question. Here: Gewitter (thunderstorm), so the concert is later.
cards.lead: You can ask back when you listen. Now we read: a short newspaper report about the festival, and five W-questions that find all the facts.

examples.de: Am Samstag gibt es ein Gewitter.
examples.en: On Saturday there is a thunderstorm.

examples.de: Deshalb tritt die Band erst um 22 Uhr auf.
examples.en: So the band only performs at 10 pm.

examples.de: Die Besucher sollen im Zelt bleiben.
examples.en: The visitors are to stay in the tent.

deeper.text: In reports erst + time means not before: erst um 22 Uhr = only at 10 pm, later than planned. Also notice: German reports like to start with the time or place, then the verb, then the subject: Am Samstag gibt es …. And sollen here means the organisers say so. The verb stattfinden (to take place) is typical for reports: Das Konzert findet am Samstag statt.

example.de: Das Konzert findet am Samstag statt.
example.en: The concert takes place on Saturday.

cards.more: Think of a detective with a notebook. The notebook has five lines: Wer? Was? Wann? Wo? Warum? The detective reads the report and writes one or two words on each line: Die Nachteulen – spielen später – Samstag, 22 Uhr – Sommerfestival bei Kiel – Gewitter. Now the whole story fits on a small card. You do not need every word of the report, only the five answers.
steps: Schlagzeile: Sommerfestival bei Kiel: Konzert am Samstag später
Am Samstag gibt es ein Gewitter. Deshalb tritt die Band „Die Nachteulen“ erst um 22 Uhr auf. Die Besucher sollen im Zelt bleiben.
Wer? Die Nachteulen, die Besucher
Was? Das Konzert ist später.
Wann? Am Samstag, um 22 Uhr. Wo? Beim Sommerfestival bei Kiel.
Warum? Es gibt ein Gewitter.

cards.title: Who is the woman who …?
cards.body: To get exact information about a person, ask Wer ist …? and add a relative clause from lesson 4: Wer ist die Frau, die das Festival leitet? (leiten = to run, to lead). The relative clause tells which person you mean, the answer gives the name.
cards.lead: The report answers Wer? with names. At the festival you also point at people you don't know. A relative clause helps you say which one.

examples.de: Wer ist die Frau, die das Festival leitet?
examples.en: Who is the woman who runs the festival?

examples.de: Wer ist der Mann, der neben Herrn Ali steht?
examples.en: Who is the man who is standing next to Herr Ali?

examples.de: Wer sind die Leute, die dort tanzen?
examples.en: Who are the people dancing over there?

deeper.text: German has a short way to ask which one: Welcher Mann? Welche Frau? But with a relative clause you give the other person a clue, so they find the right person at once. The answer often uses das with a name, even for a man or a woman: Das ist Frau Weber. Das ist der Veranstalter. Here das just points, it is not a relative pronoun.

example.de: Das ist der Veranstalter, der das Festival leitet.
example.en: That's the organiser who runs the festival.

cards.more: Picture a crowded festival field. You want to know who someone is, but you can't point with your finger, because that is rude. So you point with words: the woman who runs the festival, the man who is standing next to Herr Ali. The relative clause is your finger. Your friend follows the clue, finds the person and says the name: Das ist …. English uses who or that the same way.

cards.title: Newspaper words
cards.lead: The newspaper report used many new nouns. Before you answer questions about it, this card collects them with their articles, plus the separable verb of the topic.
cards.body: Newspapers have their own nouns: der Bericht, der Artikel, die Meldung and die Schlagzeile. People are der Leser and die Leserin; the organiser is der Veranstalter. A Rückfrage is a question to check something. The verb stattfinden is separable: Das Konzert findet am Samstag statt. The table gives the plurals.

The plural is die Artikel for both. Words for people in -er, like der Leser and der Veranstalter, add -in for women: die Leserin. The plural of the men's form does not change.

deeper.text: On the phone, the person who did not hear also often says Du bist ganz leise! or Ich höre dich nicht gut. And the person who calls may repeat the important word twice: um zehn, zehn! This repeating is normal in German phone calls. At the end Germans like to sum up once more to be sure: Also: um zehn, vor der Bühne. Bis dann!

example.de: Also um zehn, vor der Bühne. Bis dann!
example.en: So: at ten, in front of the stage. See you then!

cards.more: Think of the call as a game of ping-pong with a broken net. Anna hits the ball: the concert starts at ten. The ball gets stuck in the net, the bad connection. Leon sends back a short ball: Wann? Anna hits again, a bit slower: um zehn! At the end Leon catches the ball and says it back once more, so both know the score: Habe ich das richtig verstanden? Then they can both hang up happy.
steps: Anna: Leon? Die Verbindung ist schlecht! Das Konzert fängt erst um zehn an.
Leon: Wann? Ich höre dich nicht gut.
Anna: Um zehn! Wir treffen uns vor der Bühne.
Leon: Wo genau?
Anna: Vor der Bühne! Und Ben kommt auch. – Leon: Wer?
Leon: Ah, Ben. Habe ich das richtig verstanden: um zehn, vor der Bühne? – Anna: Genau! Bis dann!

lessons.title: Das Bild, das Anna malt: relative clauses (accusative)
lessons.goal: Talk about painting and describe things with accusative relative clauses: den, die, das, die.

grammar.topic: relative clauses in the accusative: den, die, das, die
grammar.point: When the noun is the object in the side sentence, the relative pronoun is in the accusative: den (m), die (f), das (n), die (pl). Only masculine changes (der → den). Choose by asking who does the action: the pronoun itself → nominative der; someone else (ich, Anna) → accusative den. Verb, Perfekt helper or modal at the end.
grammar.oneLine: Das ist der Maler, den ich mag.

mistake.wrong: Das ist der Maler, der ich mag.
mistake.right: Das ist der Maler, den ich mag.
mistake.why: ich is the subject of mag; the pronoun is the object, so a masculine noun needs accusative den.

terms.meaning: den / die / das / die: the pronoun is the object of the relative clause
the one who does the action after the comma: ich, Anna, man
pronoun does the action → der; someone else does it → den

cards.title: Before we start: from 'der Sänger, der …' to 'der Sänger, den ich mag'
cards.body: Anna has a small Atelier (studio) in her room, and Ben comes in to look at her pictures. He wants to say: That's the picture you are painting. You already know der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt. Today the noun is not the one doing the action. Someone else does it, and der turns into den.
steps: You already know: Das ist der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt. And from A1: Ich mag den Sänger.
New today: Das ist der Sänger, den ich mag. The pronoun is the object, so it is in the accusative.
By the end you can: talk about painting and choose der or den in a relative clause.

examples.de: Das ist der Sänger, der aus Hamburg kommt.
examples.en: That's the singer who comes from Hamburg.
examples.why: You know this: der does the action.

examples.de: Ich mag den Sänger.
examples.en: I like the singer.
examples.why: You know this from A1: the object takes den.

examples.de: Das ist der Sänger, den ich mag.
examples.en: That's the singer I like.
examples.why: New today: ich does the liking, so the pronoun is den.

cards.more: Think of a football pass. In the side sentence, someone kicks the ball. If the pronoun kicks, it is the player: der, nominative. If somebody else kicks and the pronoun is the ball, it is the object: den, accusative. You already did this in normal sentences with den Mann. Now you do it after a comma. Good news: only the masculine word changes. die, das and die stay the same.

cards.title: Painting words
cards.body: Before we join sentences, we need words for painting. der Maler or die Malerin paints. Anna malt mit dem Pinsel auf eine Leinwand. A finished picture is ein Bild or, more formal, ein Gemälde. Anna paints people: Porträts. She also paints nature: Landschaften. die Farbe means both colour and paint.
cards.lead: The intro showed Anna's Atelier. First we collect the words Ben needs there: who paints, with what, on what, and which kinds of pictures.

examples.de: Anna malt gern.
examples.en: Anna likes painting.

examples.de: Sie malt mit dem Pinsel auf eine Leinwand.
examples.en: She paints with a brush on a canvas.

examples.de: Sie malt Porträts und Landschaften.
examples.en: She paints portraits and landscapes.

deeper.text: das Bild is the everyday word: on a wall, in a book, on the Handy. das Gemälde is only a painted picture, usually with oil or acrylic paint, and sounds a bit more serious, like in a museum. A der Künstler or die Künstlerin is any artist: painter, singer or actor. So every Malerin is a Künstlerin, but not every Künstlerin is a Malerin.

example.de: Das ist kein Foto, das ist ein Gemälde.
example.en: That's not a photo, that's a painting.

cards.more: Picture Anna's room as a little shop window. On the left a box with der Pinsel, in the middle the white die Leinwand, on the right many tubes of die Farbe. On the wall hang finished pictures. Some show faces: Porträts. Some show fields and the sea near Kiel: Landschaften. When a picture hangs in die Galerie or a museum and people pay for it, it becomes ein Kunstwerk.

cards.title: Two sentences become one: the object version
cards.body: Das ist das Bild. Anna malt das Bild. In the second sentence, Anna is the subject and das Bild is the object. Join them as before: comma, pronoun, verb at the end. The pronoun now stands for the object: Das ist das Bild, das Anna malt. With a masculine noun you hear it: den Pinsel → den.
cards.lead: You have the painting words. Now the main trick of today: join two sentences when the noun is the object in the second one.

examples.de: Das ist das Bild. Anna malt das Bild.
examples.en: That's the picture. Anna is painting the picture.

examples.de: Das ist das Bild, das Anna malt.
examples.en: That's the picture Anna is painting.

examples.de: Das ist der Pinsel. Anna braucht den Pinsel.
examples.en: That's the brush. Anna needs the brush.

examples.de: Das ist der Pinsel, den Anna braucht.
examples.en: That's the brush that Anna needs.

deeper.text: Look at the second sentence before you join. Ask: what form does the noun have there? Anna braucht den Pinsel: den. That exact form becomes the pronoun. So the pronoun copies two things: the gender from the noun before the comma, and the case from its job in the side sentence. In English you can drop the word: the brush Anna needs. In German the pronoun must stay.

example.de: Das ist der Künstler, den Mira kennt.
example.en: That's the artist Mira knows.

cards.more: Think of copy and paste. You copy the noun form from the second sentence: den Pinsel. You cut the noun, keep the little word den and paste it right after the comma. Then you push the verb to the end of the sentence, like after weil. Nothing else moves. Anna stays the subject, she still does the action. Only the order changes, so the sentence sounds like one smooth thought.
steps: Find the same noun in both sentences.
Look at its form in the second sentence: den Pinsel.
Keep only den, put a comma before it.
Send the verb to the end.

cards.title: The accusative pronouns: den, die, das, die
cards.body: In the accusative the relative pronoun is den for masculine, die for feminine, das for neuter and die for plural. Only the masculine form changes: der → den. die, das and die look exactly like the nominative ones. So the only real question is: is it masculine and the object? Then den.
cards.lead: Two examples showed das and den. Here is the full set for objects in a table, and you will see that only one word is new.

examples.de: Das ist der Maler, den ich mag.
examples.en: That's the painter I like.

examples.de: Das ist die Landschaft, die Anna malt.
examples.en: That's the landscape Anna is painting.

examples.de: Das sind die Farben, die sie kauft.
examples.en: Those are the colours she buys.

deeper.text: This is the same pattern as der, die, das after a verb in A1: Ich sehe den Mann, die Frau, das Kind, die Kinder. The relative pronoun simply uses these article forms. That is why it is easy to check: put the noun after Ich sehe … and listen. Ich sehe den Pinsel → den. Ich sehe die Galerie → die.

example.de: Das ist die Galerie, die Leon gut findet.
example.en: That's the gallery Leon likes.

cards.more: Imagine four doors in a row: masculine, feminine, neuter, plural. In the nominative the signs say der, die, das, die. Now someone walks along and repaints only the first sign: den. The other three doors keep their old signs. So when you write an object relative clause, you only stop at the first door. If the noun is not masculine, just take the same word as in the nominative.

cards.title: Nominative or accusative?
cards.body: Ask who does the action in the side sentence. If the pronoun itself does it, it is the subject: der. If another subject is there, like ich or Anna, the pronoun is the object: den. Der Maler, der in Wien wohnt: the painter lives there. Der Maler, den Anna mag: Anna likes him.
cards.lead: Now you know both sets: der for subjects, den for objects. This card shows how to choose quickly when you write a masculine noun.

examples.en: The painter who lives in Vienna paints landscapes.

examples.de: Der Maler, den Anna mag, kommt aus Wien.
examples.en: The painter Anna likes comes from Vienna.

examples.de: Das ist der Künstler, der das Bild malt.
examples.en: That's the artist who is painting the picture.

examples.de: Das ist der Künstler, den ich kenne.
examples.en: That's the artist I know.

deeper.text: A quick test: count the subjects. In …, den Anna mag there is already a subject, Anna, with the verb mag. A verb has only one subject, so the pronoun must be the object. In …, der in Wien wohnt nobody else is named: the painter himself lives there, so the pronoun is the subject. Watch the verb ending too: ich kenne, Anna mag.

example.de: Das ist der Pinsel, der auf dem Tisch liegt.
example.en: That's the brush that is lying on the table.

cards.more: Think of a theatre stage in the side sentence. Every verb needs one main actor, the subject. Look at the stage after the comma. Is there already a person standing there, like ich, du or Anna? Then the pronoun cannot be the actor too. It is the thing the actor holds or sees: den. Is the stage empty except for the pronoun? Then the pronoun is the actor: der.

cards.title: Perfekt and modal verbs at the end
cards.body: Accusative relative clauses work with Perfekt and modal verbs too. The helper verb or the modal goes to the very end, after the participle or the infinitive: Das ist das Porträt, das Anna gemalt hat. Das ist die Galerie, die ich besuchen will. You know this from nominative relatives.
cards.lead: You can choose der or den now. Next we add the long verbs you know: Perfekt and modals also go to the end of an accusative relative clause.

examples.de: Das ist das Porträt, das Anna gemalt hat.
examples.en: That's the portrait Anna painted.

examples.de: Das ist die Galerie, die ich besuchen will.
examples.en: That's the gallery I want to visit.

examples.de: Das ist das Kunstwerk, das man in Wien sehen kann.
examples.en: That's the work of art you can see in Vienna.

deeper.text: Normally the helper verb stands in position two: Anna hat das Porträt gemalt. In a relative clause the two verb parts swap order and both go to the end: … gemalt hat. The finite verb, the one with the ending, is always the very last word. The same is true with separable verbs: … den Anna anruft. The verb parts join again at the end.

example.de: Das ist der Künstler, den Ben morgen anruft.
example.en: That's the artist Ben is calling tomorrow.

cards.more: Picture a train. The engine is the finite verb: hat, will, kann. In a normal sentence the engine pulls from position two. In a relative clause the train is pushed instead, so the engine goes to the back. The wagons with gemalt or besuchen stay just before it. If you read your sentence and the last word is not hat, will or kann, the engine is in the wrong place.

cards.title: In Anna's Atelier
cards.body: Ben visits Anna in her Atelier. Read the dialogue and find four relative clauses. Two are nominative: the pronoun does the action. Two are accusative: Ben or Anna does the action, and the pronoun is the object. Look at the masculine nouns: der Pinsel, der … and der Maler, den ….
cards.lead: All the parts are ready: painting words, der or den, and long verbs at the end. Now Anna and Ben use them together in a real talk.

examples.de: Ben: Ist das das Bild, das du gestern gemalt hast?
examples.en: Ben: Is that the picture you painted yesterday?

examples.de: Anna: Ja. Und das ist die Farbe, die ich am liebsten mag.
examples.en: Anna: Yes. And that's the colour I like best.

examples.de: Ben: Und der Pinsel, der so alt aussieht?
examples.en: Ben: And the brush that looks so old?

examples.de: Anna: Das ist mein Pinsel, der immer am besten malt.
examples.en: Anna: That's my brush that always paints best.

examples.de: Ben: Wer ist der Maler, den du so gern magst?
examples.en: Ben: Who is the painter you like so much?

examples.de: Anna: Das ist Franz Marc. Er hat oft Pferde gemalt.
examples.en: Anna: That's Franz Marc. He often painted horses.

deeper.text: In real talk, a relative clause often answers a short question like Welches Bild? or Welcher Pinsel?. Ben can point and ask Welcher?, and Anna answers with the noun plus a relative clause. Also notice: Anna says mein Pinsel, der …. The pronoun copies the gender of Pinsel, not of the word mein. A relative clause works after any article.

example.de: Welches Bild? Das Bild, das ich gestern gemalt habe.
example.en: Which picture? The picture I painted yesterday.

cards.more: Think of the dialogue as pointing with a finger. Ben points at things in the room, and each relative clause is a little label: the picture you painted yesterday, the colour I like best, the old brush. Without the labels, Ben would have to say Das Bild. Du hast es gestern gemalt. That works, but it sounds like a robot. With relative clauses the talk flows, the way friends really speak.

lessons.title: Vorne, hinten, in der Mitte: describing a picture
lessons.goal: Describe a picture so someone else can imagine it: place words, Man sieht …, relative clauses for details, wirken + adjective.

grammar.topic: describing a picture: place words, verb second, relative clauses for details
grammar.point: Start with the place (vorne, hinten, links, rechts, oben, unten, in der Mitte, im Vordergrund, im Hintergrund), then the verb in position 2, then the subject: Im Vordergrund sieht man … . Add details with relative clauses (der/den …) and the mood with wirken + adjective without an ending.

mistake.wrong: Im Vordergrund man sieht ein Zelt.
mistake.right: Im Vordergrund sieht man ein Zelt.
mistake.why: The place is in position 1, so the verb must come second, before man.

terms.meaning: in the foreground: what looks close, vorne
in the background: what looks far away, hinten
to seem, to look: your impression of a picture (wirkt ruhig)

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch' to 'Im Vordergrund sieht man …'
cards.body: Anna has painted the WG at the festival. Leon has not seen it yet, so Mira describes the picture to him on the phone. He cannot see it, so she must say where everything is. You know place words from your room. Today you use them for a picture, and you add details with relative clauses.
steps: You already know: Links ist ein Baum. Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. And: Das ist das Bild, das Anna malt.
New today: Im Vordergrund sieht man eine Frau, die tanzt. Place first, then the verb, then the details.
By the end you can: describe a picture step by step so another person can imagine it.

examples.de: Links ist ein Baum.
examples.en: On the left there is a tree.
examples.why: You know this: place word, verb second.

examples.de: Das ist das Bild, das Anna malt.
examples.en: That's the picture Anna is painting.
examples.why: You know this from the last lesson.

examples.de: Im Vordergrund sieht man eine Frau, die tanzt.
examples.en: In the foreground you can see a woman who is dancing.
examples.why: New today: picture place + Man sieht + a detail.

cards.more: Think of a radio reporter at a football game. The listeners see nothing, so the reporter always says where things happen: left, right, in front of the goal. Describing a picture is the same job. You are the reporter, and your friend has only your words. If you start every sentence with a place, your friend can build the picture in their head, piece by piece, like a puzzle.

cards.title: The picture map
cards.body: Put an invisible 3 × 3 grid on the picture. The top row is oben: oben links, oben, oben rechts. The middle row is links, in der Mitte, rechts. The bottom row is unten. Depth works differently: what is close is vorne, im Vordergrund; what is far away is hinten, im Hintergrund.
cards.lead: The intro showed Mira on the phone with Leon. First she needs a map of the picture, so every thing gets a clear place.

examples.de: Oben links ist der Himmel.
examples.en: At the top left is the sky.

examples.de: In der Mitte ist eine Bühne.
examples.en: In the middle there is a stage.

examples.de: Unten rechts ist eine Wiese.
examples.en: At the bottom right there is a meadow.

deeper.text: oben and unten describe the flat picture, like a page. vorne and hinten describe the room inside the picture, how near or far things look. Often both mean almost the same: things at the bottom are usually close, so unten = vorne. But a tall tree can be vorne and still reach oben. der Vordergrund and der Hintergrund are the nouns, always with im: im Vordergrund.

example.de: Im Hintergrund sieht man einen Baum.
example.en: In the background you can see a tree.

cards.more: Picture a stage in a theatre. The actors who stand right at the edge, near the audience, are vorne, im Vordergrund. The painted wall at the back of the stage is hinten, im Hintergrund. Now take a photo of this stage. On the photo, the back wall is also at the top, and the actors' feet are at the bottom. That is why vorne often looks like unten in a picture.

cards.title: Start with the place: verb second
cards.body: In a description, start most sentences with the place. Then the verb comes second and the subject comes after it: Im Vordergrund sieht man ein Zelt. In der Mitte steht eine Bühne. Useful verbs: sein, stehen, liegen, sitzen and man sieht. This keeps the listener on the map.
cards.lead: Now every part of the picture has a name. This card shows the sentence shape you use for each part: place first, then the verb.

examples.de: Im Vordergrund sieht man ein Zelt.
examples.en: In the foreground you can see a tent.

examples.de: In der Mitte steht eine Bühne.
examples.en: In the middle there is a stage.

examples.de: Im Hintergrund ist der Himmel dunkel.
examples.en: In the background the sky is dark.

deeper.text: sehen takes the accusative: Man sieht einen Baum (der Baum becomes einen). With ist, steht or liegt the thing is the subject, so it stays nominative: Da steht ein Baum. English often uses there is for both. German prefers a real verb: tall things stehen, flat things liegen, people sitzen. So choose the verb that fits the picture.

example.de: Rechts liegt eine Decke auf der Wiese.
example.en: On the right a blanket is lying on the meadow.

cards.more: Think of a tour guide in a museum. She never starts with Man sieht. She points first: Hier links …, Dort hinten …. The visitors turn their heads, and only then she says what is there. Your sentences do the same: the place word is the finger, and the verb follows right after it in position two. The subject has to wait in position three.
steps: Position 1: the place (Im Vordergrund).
Position 2: the verb (sieht, steht, ist).
Position 3: the subject (man, eine Bühne).
Then the rest.

cards.title: Describing a picture: five steps
cards.body: A good description has five steps. 1 The topic: Auf dem Bild sieht man …. 2 From front to back: vorne, in der Mitte, hinten. 3 Details with relative clauses. 4 Colours and mood: Das Bild wirkt fröhlich. 5 Your opinion: Mir gefällt besonders …, weil …. fröhlich means cheerful.
cards.lead: You can now say where things are. This card puts those sentences in a smart order, so the whole description is easy to follow.

examples.de: Auf dem Bild sieht man ein Festival.
examples.en: In the picture you can see a festival.

examples.de: Das Bild stellt die WG auf dem Festival dar.
examples.en: The picture shows the WG at the festival.

examples.de: Mir gefällt besonders die Bühne, weil sie so bunt ist.
examples.en: I especially like the stage because it is so colourful.

deeper.text: The verb darstellen is separable: Das Bild stellt die WG dar. It is more exact than zeigen and you find it in every exam. Step 1 gives the big topic in one sentence, never details. Many learners start with tiny things and the listener gets lost. Start big, then go small. In step 5 use weil: the opinion needs a reason.

example.de: Das Bild zeigt eine Landschaft bei Kiel.
example.en: The picture shows a landscape near Kiel.

cards.more: Think of a camera zoom. Step 1 is the wide shot: the whole festival. Step 2 moves the camera from the front to the back. Step 3 zooms in on single people: a man who plays the guitar. Step 4 changes the filter: is the picture warm, cold, happy or sad? Step 5 turns the camera around to you, and you say what you think about it.
steps: 1 Thema: Auf dem Bild sieht man …
2 Vorne → hinten: im Vordergrund, in der Mitte, im Hintergrund
3 Details: …, der / den / die / das …
4 Farben und Stimmung: Das Bild wirkt …
5 Meine Meinung: Mir gefällt besonders …, weil …

cards.title: Details with relative clauses
cards.body: Step 3 adds details, and relative clauses are perfect for them. Start with a place, name a person or thing, then add a comma and a relative clause: Links sieht man einen Mann, der Gitarre spielt. Choose der for a subject and den for an object, as in the last lesson.
cards.lead: Step 3 of the plan was details. Here you join the place sentences with the relative clauses from the last two lessons.

examples.de: Links sieht man einen Mann, der Gitarre spielt.
examples.en: On the left you can see a man who is playing the guitar.

examples.de: In der Mitte ist eine Frau, die tanzt.
examples.en: In the middle there is a woman who is dancing.

examples.de: Rechts steht ein Baum, den Anna sehr groß gemalt hat.
examples.en: On the right there is a tree that Anna painted very big.

deeper.text: Careful: man sieht einen Mann is accusative, but the relative pronoun is chosen fresh in its own clause. einen Mann, der Gitarre spielt: in the side sentence the man plays, so der. The case of the noun outside does not matter. In pictures, die Figur means any person drawn in it: Die Figur, die rechts steht, ist Ben.

example.de: Die Figur, die rechts steht, ist Ben.
example.en: The figure that is standing on the right is Ben.

cards.more: Think of sticky notes on a photo. The place word tells your friend where to look: links. The noun says what is there: einen Mann. The relative clause is the sticky note with extra information: der Gitarre spielt. Without the note your friend sees only a man. With it, they see a man with a guitar, maybe even hear the music. One clause per thing is enough.

rows: in der Mitte ist eine Frau

cards.title: Colours and mood: wirken
cards.body: For step 4 use wirken: to seem, to look. Das Bild wirkt fröhlich. Die Farben wirken warm. After wirken the adjective has no ending. But an adjective before a noun after der, die or das needs its ending: der blaue Himmel, die dunklen Wolken.
cards.lead: You can place things and add details. Now the feeling of the picture: colours and mood, with the verb wirken and adjectives you know.

examples.de: Das Bild wirkt fröhlich.
examples.en: The picture looks cheerful.

examples.de: Der blaue Himmel wirkt ruhig.
examples.en: The blue sky looks calm.

examples.de: Die dunklen Wolken wirken traurig.
examples.en: The dark clouds look sad.

deeper.text: wirken tells how something feels to you, not what it really is. Der Himmel ist blau is a fact. Der Himmel wirkt ruhig is your impression. That is why wirken is the key verb for step 4. Note dunkel loses its e before an ending: die dunklen Wolken. With der Nebel a picture often wirkt traurig or ruhig.

example.de: Mit dem Nebel wirkt die Landschaft sehr ruhig.
example.en: With the fog the landscape looks very calm.

cards.more: Think of the same street on two days. On a sunny day with a blue sky, people say: Die Straße wirkt fröhlich. On a grey day with fog, the same street wirkt traurig. Nothing in the street has changed. Only the colours and the light are different. A painter uses this on purpose, and you use wirken to say what the colours do to you.

cards.title: Words for the landscape in a picture
cards.lead: The five-step plan needs words for what is in a landscape. Here are the nouns of the lesson, each with its article and plural, so your description has material.
cards.body: Nouns with article: die Wiese (meadow), der Baum (tree), der Himmel (sky), der Nebel (fog) and die Figur, a person or animal drawn in a picture. The adverb vorne means at the front. Painters use these words in every landscape: Auf der Wiese steht ein Baum. Learn each article, then say one place sentence.

examples.de: Auf der Wiese steht ein Baum.
examples.en: On the meadow there is a tree.

examples.de: Der Himmel ist grau, und im Hintergrund ist Nebel.
examples.en: The sky is grey, and in the background there is fog.

examples.de: Vorne sieht man eine Figur.
examples.en: At the front you can see a figure.

deeper.text: der Baum has an umlaut in the plural: die Bäume. die Wiese and die Figur just add -n or -en. der Himmel means sky and also heaven, and der Nebel is mostly used in the singular. For where something is, German uses a two-way preposition with the dative: auf der Wiese, unter dem Baum. The place word stays in position 1 and the verb comes second.

example.de: Unter dem Baum liegt eine Decke.
example.en: A blanket lies under the tree.

cards.more: Imagine you stand in front of a picture of the festival field. At your feet is die Wiese. Next to the tent grows one Baum. Above everything hangs der Himmel, and far behind lies der Nebel. In the middle a person walks: die Figur. Walk through the picture like a camera, from the grass up to the sky, and say one short sentence for each word. Put the place first, then the verb, then the thing.

cards.title: Mira describes Anna's festival picture
cards.body: Here is Mira's description for Leon. Read it and find the five steps: topic, front to back, details with relative clauses, colours with wirken and her opinion. Every sentence about a place starts with the place word. Look for one nominative and one accusative relative clause.
cards.lead: All five steps are ready. Now Mira uses them in one full description, the kind you will write yourself on the practice day.

examples.de: Auf dem Bild sieht man die WG auf dem Festival.
examples.en: In the picture you can see the WG at the festival.

examples.de: Im Vordergrund steht unser Zelt auf einer Wiese.
examples.en: In the foreground our tent is standing on a meadow.

examples.de: In der Mitte sieht man Ben, der Gitarre spielt.
examples.en: In the middle you can see Ben, who is playing the guitar.

examples.de: Im Hintergrund ist die Bühne, die Anna sehr bunt gemalt hat.
examples.en: In the background is the stage, which Anna painted very colourfully.

examples.de: Der dunkle Himmel wirkt ein bisschen traurig, aber das Bild wirkt fröhlich.
examples.en: The dark sky looks a bit sad, but the picture looks cheerful.

examples.de: Mir gefällt besonders der Baum, weil er so groß ist.
examples.en: I especially like the tree because it's so big.

deeper.text: A description sounds natural when the sentence starts change. Mira uses Im Vordergrund, In der Mitte and Im Hintergrund, so Leon always knows where he is. In the exam, a picture description is often a speaking task: one minute, no notes. If you know the five steps by heart, you never have to think about what comes next. You only fill in the words.

example.de: Rechts sieht man Leon, den Anna nur klein gemalt hat.
example.en: On the right you can see Leon, whom Anna painted only small.

cards.more: Think of Leon on the phone with his eyes closed. After Mira's first sentence he sees a festival. After the second, a tent on green grass. Then Ben with his guitar, then a colourful stage far back, then a dark sky. At the end Leon knows the picture well enough to draw it himself. That is the real test of a good description: can the listener draw it?

lessons.title: Mein Lieblingsbild: painting yesterday and today
lessons.goal: Talk about three famous German pictures, painting today and your favourite picture, using relative clauses and indefinite pronouns.

grammar.topic: the whole chapter combined: relative clauses (nominative + accusative), indefinite pronouns, Perfekt
grammar.point: Describe famous pictures with relative clauses: Das ist ein Bild, das Albrecht Dürer gemalt hat (helper verb last). Talk about painters' lives in the Perfekt. Use indefinite pronouns for people: alle, jemand, niemand (no nicht).

terms.meaning: the real picture the painter made; everything else is a copy
what a picture shows: a hare, a horse, a landscape
chunk: I especially like …; the verb matches the thing you like

cards.title: Before we start: from Anna's picture to famous pictures
cards.body: Herr Ali wants to hang Anna's festival picture in the restaurant „Zum Löwen“. Frau Weber is happy and tells everyone about her own favourite picture in Hamburg. Today you meet three famous German painters and their pictures. You talk about painting today and about your own favourite picture, with everything from this chapter.
steps: You already know: Das ist das Bild, das Anna gemalt hat. Im Vordergrund sieht man …
New today: Das ist ein Bild, das Albrecht Dürer gemalt hat. Famous pictures, painting today, your favourite picture.
By the end you can: name three famous pictures, say who painted them and where they hang, and talk about your Lieblingsbild.

examples.de: Das ist ein Bild, das Albrecht Dürer gemalt hat.
examples.en: That's a picture Albrecht Dürer painted.
examples.why: New today: the same pattern for famous painters.

cards.more: Think of a small museum tour in one lesson. Room one: an old picture by a painter from Nürnberg, more than five hundred years old. Room two: a man in the fog in Hamburg. Room three: a blue horse in München. Then you leave the museum and see painting today: on a tablet, on a wall in the street. You need no new grammar for the tour. You use the relative clauses you already have.

cards.title: Albrecht Dürer: the hare
cards.body: Albrecht Dürer kommt aus Nürnberg. Der „Feldhase“ ist ein Bild, das Albrecht Dürer 1502 gemalt hat. der Feldhase is a field hare, der Hase means hare. The original is in Wien, in the Albertina, a famous museum. The hare looks so real that you want to touch it.
cards.lead: The intro opened the museum tour. The first room is the oldest: a picture of an animal that Dürer painted more than five hundred years ago.

examples.de: Albrecht Dürer kommt aus Nürnberg.
examples.en: Albrecht Dürer comes from Nuremberg.

examples.de: Der „Feldhase“ ist ein Bild, das Albrecht Dürer 1502 gemalt hat.
examples.en: The 'Feldhase' is a picture Albrecht Dürer painted in 1502.

examples.en: The original is in Vienna.

deeper.text: das Original is the real picture that the painter made. Everything else is eine Kopie: a poster, a postcard, a photo on the Handy. Very old pictures on paper do not like light, so museums often show the original only for a short time. For a painter's life, use the Perfekt you know: Er hat das Bild 1502 gemalt.

example.de: Viele Leute haben eine Kopie zu Hause.
example.en: Many people have a copy at home.

cards.more: Think of a very good photo of your cat. Every hair is there, the eyes shine, the ears stand up. Now imagine someone made that picture with a brush, by hand, more than five hundred years ago, without a camera. That is Dürer's hare. Many German children know it from posters and books, so if you say der Hase von Dürer, most Germans know the picture at once.

cards.title: Caspar David Friedrich: the man in the fog
cards.body: „Der Wanderer über dem Nebelmeer“ ist ein Bild, das Caspar David Friedrich um 1818 gemalt hat. A man stands on a rock, der Felsen, and looks into the fog. das Nebelmeer is a sea of fog. The picture hangs in the Hamburger Kunsthalle, an art museum in Hamburg. It is Frau Weber's favourite.
cards.lead: Dürer painted an animal very exactly. The next painter, Friedrich, paints a feeling: a man alone in front of a big landscape.

examples.de: Ein Mann steht auf einem Felsen.
examples.en: A man is standing on a rock.

examples.de: Er sieht in den Nebel.
examples.en: He is looking into the fog.

examples.de: Das ist das Bild, das Frau Weber am liebsten mag.
examples.en: That's the picture Frau Weber likes best.

deeper.text: The man stands with his back to us, so we do not see his face. We look in the same direction as he does. That is why many people feel they are standing there themselves. um 1818 means about 1818: the exact year is not sure. With über dem Nebelmeer you see a two-way preposition in the dative: über + dem, where something is.

example.de: Im Vordergrund steht ein Mann, den man nur von hinten sieht.
example.en: In the foreground stands a man you only see from behind.

cards.more: Think of standing on a mountain early in the morning. Down in the valley there is thick fog, white like a sea. Only the tops of the hills come out of it, like little islands. You are alone and very quiet. Friedrich painted exactly this moment. When you describe the picture, you can use every step: vorne der Mann, hinten der Nebel, and the mood: ruhig.

cards.title: Franz Marc: the blue horse
cards.body: „Blaues Pferd I“ ist ein Bild, das Franz Marc 1911 gemalt hat. It hangs in the Lenbachhaus, a museum in München. Er hat oft Tiere gemalt. Die Farben sind sehr stark. Blue for a horse? In the real world no, but Marc chose colours for the feeling, not for the facts.
cards.lead: Friedrich painted nature as we know it. Franz Marc did something new about a hundred years later: animals in colours they never have in real life.

examples.de: Franz Marc hat oft Tiere gemalt.
examples.en: Franz Marc often painted animals.

examples.de: Die Farben sind sehr stark.
examples.en: The colours are very strong.

examples.de: Ein Pferd, das blau ist? Das gibt es nur auf Bildern.
examples.en: A horse that is blue? That only exists in pictures.

deeper.text: The title has no article: „Blaues Pferd I“. So the adjective takes the ending -es, like in a strong neuter phrase. That is just the title; learn it as one name. The I is a Roman one: Marc painted more blue horses later. Compare Friedrich: his colours show nature as it looks. Marc's colours show a mood. Das Bild wirkt fröhlich und stark.

example.de: Das Bild wirkt fröhlich, weil die Farben so stark sind.
example.en: The picture looks cheerful because the colours are so strong.

cards.more: Think of how you feel on a happy day. You might say: today everything is pink. Of course nothing is really pink, but the word shows your mood. Marc did the same with paint. A blue horse is not a mistake. For Marc, blue was a strong, serious and spiritual colour. So when you look at the picture, do not ask: is it real? Ask: how does it wirken?

cards.title: Painting today
cards.body: Malerei today is not only Pinsel and Leinwand. Heute malen viele Leute am Tablet: that is digital. Einige malen Graffiti an Wänden. Others paint a Selbstporträt, a picture of themselves, or a Stillleben: fruit, flowers, a cup on a table. Anna malt mit Farbe und Pinsel, Ben malt digital.
cards.lead: The three famous pictures are old. Now we jump to today: new tools, new places to paint, and the WG friends as painters.

examples.en: Today many people paint on a tablet.

examples.de: Einige malen Graffiti an Wänden.
examples.en: Some paint graffiti on walls.

examples.de: Anna malt mit Farbe und Pinsel, Ben malt digital.
examples.en: Anna paints with paint and a brush, Ben paints digitally.

deeper.text: das Motiv is what a picture shows: a hare, a man in the fog, a blue horse. The Motiv of a Stillleben is always things that do not move. das Stillleben has a triple l: still + Leben. digital has no ending after a verb: Ben malt digital. But before a noun it needs one: ein digitales Bild, like any adjective.

example.de: Das Motiv von Annas Bild ist die WG.
example.en: The subject of Anna's picture is the WG.

cards.more: Think of a wall in a city. Fifty years ago it was grey. Today someone has painted a big colourful face on it, and people take photos in front of it. In a café, a young woman paints on her tablet with a digital pen. At home, Anna still opens her tubes of paint and cleans her brushes. All three are Malerei. Only the tools are different.

cards.title: My favourite picture
cards.body: To talk about your Lieblingsbild, answer four questions: Wie heißt es? Wer hat es gemalt? Was sieht man? Warum gefällt es dir? Indefinite pronouns help with the people around it: Niemand in der WG malt so gut wie Anna. Alle finden das Bild schön. Will jemand das Bild kaufen?
cards.lead: You now know three famous pictures and painting today. Here you put it together and talk about your own Lieblingsbild, with all of this chapter.

examples.en: My favourite picture is the 'Feldhase'.

examples.de: Will jemand das Bild kaufen?
examples.en: Does anybody want to buy the picture?

deeper.text: For step 4, Warum gefällt es dir?, use weil or a relative clause: Mir gefällt besonders der Mann, der in den Nebel sieht. Mir gefällt besonders … is a fixed chunk: the thing you like is the subject, so the verb matches it. Mir gefallen besonders die Farben: plural. And remember: niemand never takes nicht.

example.de: Mir gefallen besonders die Farben, die man auf dem Bild sieht.
example.en: I especially like the colours you see in the picture.

cards.more: Think of a dating profile for a picture. Name: „Blaues Pferd I“. Made by: Franz Marc. Looks like: a blue horse on a hill. Why we match: the colours make me happy. If you can fill in those four lines, you can talk about any picture for a whole minute. Then add one sentence about the people around you: Alle in der WG finden es schön.

Wer hat es gemalt? Das ist ein Bild, das … gemalt hat.
Was sieht man? Im Vordergrund …, im Hintergrund …
Warum gefällt es dir? Mir gefällt besonders …, weil …

cards.title: Words for Anna's show
cards.lead: Anna's show needs a few last words: where she paints, what makes a picture the real one, and the word for your own favourite. Here they are with their articles.
cards.body: Nouns with article: das Atelier is the painter's studio. das Lieblingsbild is your favourite picture: Lieblings- plus das Bild. der Hase is the hare of Dürer. das Original is the real picture, die Kopie is the copy. All four fit Anna's show in the restaurant „Zum Löwen“. Say each with its article.

deeper.text: Lieblings- can stand in front of many nouns: das Lieblingslied, die Lieblingsband, das Lieblingsessen. The last word gives the article, so Lieblingsband is feminine. Atelier comes from French: the end sounds like yeh, with a soft t (ah-te-LYEH). The plural of Original just adds -e: die Originale, but die Kopie adds -n: die Kopien.

example.en: My favourite song is playing on the radio right now.

cards.more: Imagine Anna's evening at „Zum Löwen“. She walks out of her Atelier with her picture under her arm and hangs it on the wall. Guests ask: Ist das ein Original? Anna smiles: Ja, und es ist mein Lieblingsbild. In the corner of the room hangs a poster of Dürer's Hase, a Kopie. Retell this small evening in four sentences, and use the new nouns with their articles.

cards.body: Herr Ali hangs Anna's festival picture in the restaurant „Zum Löwen“. He says du to Anna, and Anna says Sie to him. Read the dialogue and find the relative clauses and the indefinite pronouns. Notice: auf dem Festival, not am Festival.

examples.en: Herr Ali: That's the picture everyone should see!

examples.en: Anna: Thank you, Herr Ali. That's the picture I painted at the festival.

examples.en: Herr Ali: Do you like the spot here on the wall?

examples.en: Anna: Yes! Is that the place you have for me?

examples.de: Herr Ali: Genau. Hier sehen es alle Gäste.
examples.en: Herr Ali: Exactly. All the guests see it here.

examples.de: Anna: Toll! Vielleicht will jemand das Original kaufen.
examples.en: Anna: Great! Maybe someone wants to buy the original.

deeper.text: In a real talk you rarely use all steps of a description. People mix short comments with relative clauses: Das ist das Bild, das …, and indefinite pronouns: alle, jemand, niemand. That makes speech sound natural. Note der Platz, den Sie für mich haben: Sie is the subject, so den. Formal Sie and relative clauses work together without problems.

example.en: That's a picture everyone likes to see.

cards.more: Think of the first day of a small show. The picture hangs on the wall, the guests come in with their food and stop. Somebody points: Wer hat das gemalt? Herr Ali proudly says: Anna, eine Künstlerin, die oft bei uns isst. Anna stands next to it and feels a bit shy. At the end of A2, you can say all of this yourself, in German, without notes.

reading.text:
Festival-Packliste im WG-Chat

Mira: Hallo zusammen! Am Freitag fahren wir zum Sommerfestival. Hier ist meine Packliste: Zelt, Schlafsäcke, Isomatten, Taschenlampe, Becher, Snacks. Hat jemand eine Taschenlampe?

Leon: Ich habe eine. Und ich bringe zwei Klappstühle mit. Das Zelt von Frau Weber ist schon im Auto.

Ben: Ich habe keine Taschenlampe. Ich habe nichts! Kein Zelt, keinen Schlafsack, keine Isomatte. Hättest du einen Schlafsack für mich, Mira?

Mira: Ja, ich habe noch einen. Aber Becher hat niemand, oder?

Anna: Doch, ich habe welche. Und Snacks kaufe ich am Donnerstag. Alles ist schon im Auto, nur die Snacks fehlen noch.

Ben: Brauchen wir Gummistiefel?

Anna: Nein, niemand braucht Gummistiefel. Das Wetter ist gut, es gibt keinen Regen. Aber Mückenspray brauchen alle! Am See gibt es viele Mücken.

Leon: Super. Dann fahren wir am Freitag um zehn Uhr. Alle sind dabei!

Sommerfestival bei Kiel: Konzert am Samstag später

Kiel. Das Sommerfestival, das jedes Jahr am See stattfindet, hat in diesem Jahr ein Problem: Am Samstag gibt es ein Gewitter. Deshalb tritt die Band „Die Nachteulen“ erst um 22 Uhr auf, nicht um 20 Uhr.

Die Nachteulen sind eine Rockband, die aus Hamburg kommt. Die Musiker haben die Band 2019 gegründet. Ihr Album ist sehr erfolgreich. Die Sängerin, die auch die Texte schreibt, hat eine tolle Stimme.

Der Veranstalter sagt: „Wir erwarten 8000 Besucher. Alle sollen bis 22 Uhr im Zelt bleiben. Das Zelt ist groß genug.“ Für Leute, die schon um 20 Uhr da sind, gibt es dort Musik und Snacks.

Das Konzert am Sonntag findet wie geplant um 18 Uhr statt.

reading.title: Kleine Ausstellung im Restaurant „Zum Löwen“
reading.text:
Kleine Ausstellung im Restaurant „Zum Löwen“

Liebe Gäste,
ab Freitag hängen bei uns drei Bilder von Anna. Anna ist eine junge Künstlerin, die oft bei uns isst. Kommen Sie am Freitag um 19 Uhr! Es gibt Musik und einen kleinen Snack. Der Eintritt ist frei.
Herzliche Grüße
Ihr Herr Ali

1. „Unser Festival“
Das ist das Bild, das Anna auf dem Festival gemalt hat. Im Vordergrund sieht man ein Zelt, im Hintergrund eine bunte Bühne. Das Bild wirkt fröhlich.

2. „Frau Weber“
Das ist ein Porträt, das Anna im Winter gemalt hat. Frau Weber ist eine Nachbarin, die gern Klavier spielt.

3. „Am Meer bei Kiel“
Eine Landschaft mit Wiese, Himmel und Nebel. Das Original kann man kaufen.

listening.title: Mira und Ben in der Hamburger Kunsthalle
listening.script:
Mira: Schau mal, Ben! Das ist das Bild, das Frau Weber am liebsten mag.
Ben: „Der Wanderer über dem Nebelmeer“? Von Caspar David Friedrich?
Mira: Genau. Vorne sieht man einen Mann, der auf einem Felsen steht.
Ben: Und im Hintergrund sieht man nur Nebel und Berge.
Mira: Man sieht den Mann nur von hinten. Das finde ich spannend.
Ben: Das Bild wirkt sehr ruhig. Aber für mich ist es ein bisschen traurig.
Mira: Wirklich? Ich finde es schön. Was ist denn dein Lieblingsbild?
Ben: Mein Lieblingsbild ist „Blaues Pferd I“ von Franz Marc. Das hängt in München.
Mira: Ein Pferd, das blau ist? Das gibt es nur auf Bildern!
Ben: Genau! Mir gefallen besonders die starken Farben.
Mira: Und mein Lieblingsbild ist der „Feldhase“ von Dürer. Das Original ist in Wien.
Ben: Dann fahren wir nächstes Jahr nach Wien!
